title: Shells, commands and arguments
body: A terminal is only a window that sends keystrokes and displays text. The shell is the program reading what you type: Bash parses each line into words, decides what each word means, runs the command, and waits for it to finish before printing the next prompt. The kernel does the real work of starting programs, opening files and moving bytes; Bash is the language that describes which of those things should happen.

A simple command is a command name followed by arguments separated by blanks (spaces or tabs). In `printf '%s\n' hello`, the name is printf and it receives two arguments. Bash, not the command, splits the line into words; the program just receives an ordered list of strings. That is why spacing matters so much in shell code, and why most later lessons are about controlling exactly where words begin and end.

echo prints its arguments separated by single spaces and followed by a newline. It is fine for fixed text, but its handling of options such as -n and -e and of backslashes differs between shells and settings. printf is the predictable tool: the first argument is a format, % directives consume the remaining arguments, and nothing is added that you did not ask for — including the newline, which you write as \n.

If there are more arguments than directives, printf reuses the format until the arguments run out. That makes `printf '%s\n' a b c` print three lines, a short idiom you will use constantly for listing values one per line. %d formats integers, %s strings, %5s pads to a width, and %% prints a literal percent sign.

Every command finishes with an exit status: 0 means success and 1–255 mean some kind of failure. You will build control flow from these statuses later. For now, notice that a command which prints nothing can still succeed, and a command that prints an error message usually also returns a non-zero status. Output and success are separate channels of information.
code:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# A command is a name followed by arguments separated by blanks.
echo Hello from Bash
printf '%s has %d letters\n' Bash 4
# The format is reused while arguments remain.
printf 'item: %s\n' tea milk bread
challenge: Use one printf command to print a two-column table: the words name and score on the first line, then ada 95 and alan 88, each column padded to width 6.
solution:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
printf '%-6s%6s\n' name score ada 95 alan 88
question: Why is printf usually preferred over echo for exact output?
correct: Its format controls every byte, including whether a newline is printed
wrong: It runs faster because it is not a builtin
It splits words differently from every other command
reasoning: printf follows its format exactly and reuses it for extra arguments; echo option and backslash handling varies between shells and settings.
expectedStdout:
Hello from Bash
Bash has 4 letters
item: tea
item: milk
item: bread

title: Builtins, keywords, functions and programs
body: Not every command is a separate program on disk. A builtin such as cd, printf or read is implemented inside Bash itself. Some must be builtins: cd has to change the current shell's directory, and a child process could only change its own. A keyword such as if, for, [[ or { is part of the grammar and is recognized only at the start of a command.

Bash looks a name up in a fixed order: aliases (only in interactive shells by default), keywords, functions, builtins, and finally executable files found by searching the directories in PATH. The first match wins. A function named ls would therefore hide the ls program until you remove it or bypass it.

type tells you which kind of thing a name is. type -t prints a single word — alias, keyword, function, builtin or file — which is easy to test in scripts. type -a lists every definition along the search order, and command -v prints how the name would be invoked or nothing when it cannot be found.

help prints documentation for builtins and keywords (help printf, help '[['), while man documents external programs. Because both exist, always check type first when documentation does not match what you see: the printf builtin and the /usr/bin/printf program are different implementations.

The command builtin runs a name while skipping functions, and builtin forces a builtin. These are the standard ways to write a wrapper function named like the thing it wraps without calling itself forever.
challenge: Write a function named printf that prefixes every call with "> " and then forwards all of its arguments to the real printf builtin. Call it once with the format '%s\n' and the word wrapped.
question: In what order does Bash search for a command name?
correct: Aliases, keywords, functions, builtins, then PATH directories
wrong: Only PATH directories; builtins are files too
reasoning: The first match wins, so a function can hide a builtin or program; type -t reveals which kind a name resolves to.
expectedStdout:
if     -> keyword
printf -> builtin
greet  -> function
ls     -> file
now in demo

title: Scripts, the shebang line and permissions
body: A script is a text file of commands. You can always run it as `bash script.sh`: Bash is the program and the file is its input. To run it as `./script.sh`, the file needs execute permission and a first line telling the kernel which interpreter to use.

That first line is the shebang: #! followed by an interpreter path. `#!/usr/bin/env bash` asks env to find bash on PATH, which picks up a newer Homebrew or system Bash instead of hard-coding /bin/bash — on macOS /bin/bash is still version 3.2 from 2007. Use `#!/bin/sh` only for scripts that really are POSIX sh, since sh may be dash, ash or Bash in POSIX mode.

chmod +x adds execute permission. ls -l shows permissions as three rwx triples for the owner, group and others. Without x, the kernel refuses to execute the file and Bash reports "Permission denied" with status 126; when the name is not found at all the status is 127.

The current directory is not searched for commands unless it is in PATH, and putting . in PATH is a security risk. That is why you type ./script.sh: the slash makes Bash execute that exact path instead of searching.

Inside a script, $0 is the name used to invoke it and the script ends with the status of its last command unless you call exit N explicitly. A script runs in a new process, so variables it sets and directories it changes do not affect the shell that started it. Use `source file` (or `. file`) when you deliberately want a file to run in the current shell.
code:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# shellcheck disable=SC2016  # $0 must stay literal: the new script expands it
printf '#!/usr/bin/env bash\necho "running ${0##*/}"\n' > hello.sh
./hello.sh 2>/dev/null || printf 'status %d: not executable yet\n' "$?"
chmod +x hello.sh
./hello.sh
bash hello.sh
challenge: Create a script named setdir.sh containing `cd /` . Run it with bash, then source it, and print the base name of $PWD after each — show that only sourcing changes the current shell.
solution:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
mkdir -p work && cd work || exit
printf 'cd /\n' > setdir.sh
bash setdir.sh
printf 'after bash: %s\n' "${PWD##*/}"
# shellcheck source=/dev/null
source ./setdir.sh
printf 'after source: %s\n' "$PWD"
question: Why does running ./script.sh that changes directory leave your shell where it was?
correct: The script runs in a child process with its own working directory
wrong: The shebang resets the directory afterwards
Only root can change directories in scripts
reasoning: Executing a file starts a new process; its directory and variables vanish with it. source runs the file in the current shell instead.
expectedStdout:
status 126: not executable yet
running hello.sh
running hello.sh

title: PATH and how programs are found
body: PATH is a colon-separated list of directories. When a command name contains no slash and is not an alias, keyword, function or builtin, Bash tries each PATH directory from left to right and runs the first executable file with that name.

Order is behaviour: prepending a directory lets its programs override system ones, which is how version managers and Homebrew work. Appending is safer when you only want to add new commands. An empty element (a leading or trailing colon, or ::) means the current directory, which is a classic accident.

Bash remembers where it found programs in a hash table to avoid repeated searches. hash lists the table and hash -r clears it. If you install a program earlier on PATH during a session and Bash still runs the old one, a stale hash entry is the usual reason. Assigning PATH also clears the table.

A variable assignment written immediately before a command applies only to that command's environment: `PATH=/opt/bin tool` changes PATH for tool alone. Plain `PATH=...` on its own line changes it for the rest of the script.

Scripts that run under cron, launchd, sudo or CI often receive a much shorter PATH than your interactive shell. Robust scripts either set PATH explicitly at the top or check for required tools with command -v and fail with a clear message.
code:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
mkdir -p tools
printf '#!/usr/bin/env bash\necho "local tool"\n' > tools/sort
chmod +x tools/sort
printf '%s\n' b a | sort
# Prepend the directory: our sort now wins the PATH search.
PATH="$PWD/tools:$PATH"
printf '%s\n' b a | sort
type -t sort
command -v nosuchcommand || echo 'nosuchcommand: not found'
challenge: Write a script that checks for the commands sort, awk and nosuchtool using command -v, printing "ok NAME" or "missing NAME" for each, and exits with status 1 if any were missing.
solution:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
missing=0
for tool in sort awk nosuchtool; do
    if command -v "$tool" >/dev/null; then
        echo "ok $tool"
    else
        echo "missing $tool"
        missing=1
    fi
done
exit "$missing"
question: What does an empty element in PATH, such as a trailing colon, mean?
correct: The current directory is searched
reasoning: An empty PATH element means the current directory, an easy accidental security hole; write directories explicitly.
expectedStdout:
a
b
local tool
file
nosuchcommand: not found
solutionStdout:
ok sort
ok awk
missing nosuchtool

title: Lines, comments and command lists
body: Bash reads input line by line, but a command can span lines when a construct is unfinished — an open quote, a pipe at line end, an if without fi — or when a line ends with a backslash. A backslash-newline pair is removed entirely, so it must be the very last character; a trailing space after it breaks the continuation.
A # at the start of a word begins a comment that runs to the end of the line. Inside quotes or in the middle of a word (like file#1) it is an ordinary character.

A list is a sequence of commands separated by ;, &, && or || and ended by ;, & or a newline. ; runs commands one after another. && runs the right side only if the left succeeded; || runs it only if the left failed. & runs the left side in the background without waiting.
&& and || have equal precedence and group left to right, so `a && b || c` runs c when either a or b fails — it is not an if/else. Use a real if statement when you mean if/else.

Braces { list; } group commands in the current shell, so redirections or && can apply to the whole group; the spaces and the final ; or newline are required because { and } are keywords. Parentheses ( list ) run the group in a subshell, an isolated copy of the shell.
code:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
echo one; echo two   # two commands on one line
printf '%s ' this command \
    continues here
echo
true && echo 'after success'
false || echo 'after failure'
# Grouping lets one redirection capture several commands.
{ echo first; echo second; } > both.txt
cat both.txt
# a && b || c is not if/else: c runs when b fails too.
true && false || echo 'c ran even though a succeeded'
challenge: Write one command list that creates a directory named out, enters it, and writes ok to status.txt only if both earlier steps succeed; if any step fails print "setup failed". Finish by printing the contents of out/status.txt.
solution:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
if mkdir -p out && cd out && echo ok > status.txt; then
    cd ..
else
    echo 'setup failed'
fi
cat out/status.txt
question: When does c run in `a && b || c`?
correct: When a fails or when a succeeds and b fails
reasoning: && and || have equal precedence and are left-associative; the expression is (a && b) || c, so it is not a safe if/else.
expectedStdout:
one
two
this command continues here 
after success
after failure
first
second
c ran even though a succeeded

title: Single quotes, double quotes and backslashes
body: Quoting removes the special meaning of characters. Bash has three mechanisms: a backslash protects the single next character; single quotes protect everything up to the next single quote; double quotes protect everything except $, ` (backquote), \ in some positions, and ! in interactive history expansion.

Single quotes are completely literal. Nothing expands inside them, and there is no escape: a single quote cannot appear inside single quotes. To include one, close the quotes, add an escaped quote, and reopen: 'it'\''s' produces it's.

Double quotes still allow parameter expansion ($name, ${name}), command substitution ($(...)) and arithmetic expansion ($((...))), but the result is kept as one word: no word splitting and no filename globbing happen to it. This is exactly what you want for nearly every variable use.

Quotes are not part of the value. After parsing, Bash performs quote removal, so the program receives the characters inside the quotes and never sees the quotes themselves. Adjacent quoted and unquoted pieces with no space between them join into one word: 'a'"b"c is the single argument abc.

A useful rule: single-quote fixed text, double-quote anything containing an expansion, and leave a word unquoted only when you deliberately want splitting or globbing — which is rare and deserves a comment.
code:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# shellcheck disable=SC2016  # the literal $name is the lesson
name=world
echo 'single: $name stays literal'
echo "double: hello $name"
echo escaped: \$name
echo 'it'\''s'
echo 'joined'"with"no-spaces
printf '[%s]\n' "two  spaces kept" two  spaces collapsed
challenge: Print exactly this line, using one echo command and single quotes for the literal parts: She said "it's $5"
question: What is the only character that cannot appear inside single quotes?
correct: A single quote
reasoning: Single quotes have no escape mechanism; end the quotes, add \' and reopen them, or use $'...'.
expectedStdout:
single: $name stays literal
double: hello world
escaped: $name
it's
joinedwithno-spaces
[two  spaces kept]
[two]
[spaces]
[collapsed]

title: ANSI-C quoting with $'…' and printf %q
body: $'...' is a quoting form in which backslash escapes are decoded: \n newline, \t tab, \\ backslash, \' single quote, \xHH a byte in hex, \uHHHH a Unicode code point. The result is treated as if it had been single-quoted, so no further expansion happens.
It is the clean way to put control characters in a value, for example IFS=$'\n' to split only on newlines, or a literal tab separator for cut and sort.
$"..." is a different feature: a double-quoted string looked up in a translation catalogue for the current locale. Unless your script is localized, do not use it; it is mostly confused with $'...'.

printf %q prints a value quoted so that Bash can read it back as the same single word. This is invaluable when logging commands or arguments with spaces or control characters, and when generating shell code safely. In Bash 5.3 the alternate form %#q forces single-quote style, which many people find easier to read.
Do not try to build shell commands by concatenating strings and running eval; later lessons show safer array-based approaches. When you must produce shell-readable text, %q is the tool.
code:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
row=$'name\tscore'
printf '%s\n' "$row"
printf '%s\n' "$row" | cut -f2
weird=$'two words\nand a newline'
printf '%q\n' "$weird"
printf '%q %#q\n' 'a b' 'a b'
challenge: Store a value containing a single quote, a tab and the word end (for example it's<TAB>end) using $'...', then print it with printf %q so it could be pasted back into Bash.
question: What does $'\t' produce?
correct: A literal tab character
wrong: A translated message for the locale
reasoning: $'...' decodes backslash escapes and then behaves like single quotes; $"..." is unrelated locale translation.
expectedStdout:
name	score
score
$'two words\nand a newline'
a\ b 'a b'

title: Word splitting and why to quote expansions
body: After expansions, Bash scans the results of unquoted parameter expansions, command substitutions and arithmetic expansions and splits them into separate words on the characters in IFS — by default space, tab and newline. Text that you typed literally is not re-split; only expansion results are.

Splitting is followed by pathname expansion (globbing): any resulting word containing *, ? or [ is treated as a pattern and replaced by matching file names. An unquoted $var holding "*" can therefore become a list of every file in the directory.

A third surprise: an unquoted expansion that is empty disappears entirely, so the command receives one argument fewer. `[ $x = y ]` with empty x becomes `[ = y ]`, a syntax error. Quoting keeps an empty string as an empty argument.

Quote expansions — "$var", "$(cmd)" — unless you have a specific reason not to. ShellCheck reports unquoted expansions as SC2086, one of the most common real-world bugs. When you do need several values, use an array rather than relying on splitting.
Splitting is not useless: it is how `for word in $line` or `read -a` divide text. The point is to choose it deliberately, ideally with a locally set IFS, rather than receive it by accident.
code:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# shellcheck disable=SC2086  # this lesson demonstrates unquoted expansion on purpose
touch alpha.txt beta.txt
value='two  words *.txt'
printf '[%s]\n' $value
echo ---
printf '[%s]\n' "$value"
echo ---
empty=''
printf '%s args\n' "$(set -- $empty; echo $#)" "$(set -- "$empty"; echo $#)"
challenge: A variable holds a file name with spaces: "my report.txt". Create that file, then write the safe command that counts its lines with wc -l and reads from it via input redirection, and print only the count (the file has two lines).
solution:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
file='my report.txt'
printf '%s\n' one two > "$file"
lines=$(wc -l < "$file")
echo "$((lines))"
question: Which three things can happen to an unquoted $var after expansion?
correct: It can split into several words, glob into file names, or vanish when empty
wrong: It is always passed as one argument
It is only split on spaces, never globbed
It is converted to a number
reasoning: Unquoted expansions go through word splitting, pathname expansion and empty-word removal; double quotes prevent all three.

title: Controlling IFS for deliberate splitting
body: IFS (internal field separator) decides where splitting happens. Whitespace characters in IFS are special: runs of them count as one separator and leading or trailing whitespace is ignored. Non-whitespace characters such as : or , are strict: every occurrence separates a field, so a::b has an empty middle field.

Changing IFS globally affects every later unquoted expansion and read in the script. Prefer setting it only for one command: `IFS=: read -r a b c <<< "$line"` assigns IFS for that read alone. Inside a function, `local IFS=,` confines the change to the function.

read splits the line it reads using IFS and assigns fields to the named variables, with any remainder going to the last variable. read -a puts all fields into an array. Always add -r so backslashes in the input are kept literally instead of being treated as escapes.

"$*" joins all positional parameters using the first character of IFS, which is a quick way to join values: with IFS=, it produces a,b,c. "$@" never joins; it keeps every parameter as a separate word.
An IFS set to the empty string disables splitting completely. The idiom `while IFS= read -r line` uses that to keep leading and trailing whitespace on each line exactly as it was.
code:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
line='root:x:0:0::/root:/bin/sh'
IFS=: read -r user _ uid _ _ home shell <<< "$line"
printf '%s uid=%s home=%s shell=%s\n' "$user" "$uid" "$home" "$shell"
IFS=, read -r -a parts <<< 'a,,b'
printf '%d fields\n' "${#parts[@]}"
join() { local IFS=$1; shift; echo "$*"; }
join - x y z
printf '[%s]\n' "$(IFS= read -r kept <<< '  padded  '; echo "$kept")"
challenge: Given the CSV line "ada,lovelace,1815", read it into three variables with a one-command IFS and print "lovelace, ada (1815)". Then show that IFS outside the read is unchanged by printing its length (3 for space, tab, newline).
solution:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
IFS=, read -r first last year <<< 'ada,lovelace,1815'
echo "$last, $first ($year)"
echo "${#IFS}"
question: What does `IFS=, read -r a b <<< "$line"` change?
correct: IFS only for that read command
wrong: IFS for the rest of the script
IFS for every child process forever
reasoning: An assignment before a command applies only to that command, so IFS stays at its default afterwards.

title: Metacharacters, operators and the parse order
body: Before anything runs, Bash splits input into tokens. Metacharacters — space, tab, newline, |, &, ;, (, ), < and > — end words and form operators. That is why `a>b` writes a to a file named b, and why `echo a;b` runs two commands. Quote or escape metacharacters to use them as data.

Parsing comes first, then expansion. Operators and keywords are recognized during parsing, so a variable containing ; or | is never treated as a command separator. This is why storing a whole command line in a variable and running $cmd does not work for pipes or redirections — and why that is a good thing for safety.

Expansions happen in a fixed order: brace expansion; then tilde, parameter, arithmetic and command substitution (left to right); then word splitting; then pathname expansion; finally quote removal. Knowing the order explains many puzzles, such as why {1..$n} does not work: brace expansion runs before $n is expanded.
Tilde expansion turns an unquoted ~ at the start of a word into $HOME, and ~user into that user's home directory. Inside quotes the tilde is literal, so write "$HOME/dir" rather than "~/dir".
When in doubt, print the words a command receives with printf '[%s]\n' followed by the same arguments. Seeing each argument in brackets is the fastest debugging tool for quoting problems.
code:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
cmd='echo a; echo b'
# The ; inside the variable is data, not an operator.
$cmd
n=3
# shellcheck disable=SC2051  # deliberately showing that braces expand before $n
printf '[%s] ' {1..$n}; echo
# shellcheck disable=SC2088  # showing that a quoted tilde stays literal
printf '[%s] ' "~/notes" ~nosuchuserxyz; echo
[[ ~/notes == "$HOME/notes" ]] && echo "unquoted ~ expanded to \$HOME"
challenge: Use the bracket-printing technique to show how many arguments `printf '[%s]\n' a\ b "c d" e'f g'` passes, printing each argument on its own line in brackets.
solution:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
printf '[%s]\n' a\ b "c d" e'f g'
question: Why does {1..$n} not produce a numeric range?
correct: Brace expansion runs before parameter expansion
wrong: Brace expansion is disabled in scripts
reasoning: Brace expansion is the first expansion, so it sees the literal $n; use a C-style for loop or seq instead.
expectedStdout:
a; echo b
[{1..3}] 
[~/notes] [~nosuchuserxyz] 
unquoted ~ expanded to $HOME

title: Variables, assignment and attributes
body: A variable is assigned with name=value and no spaces around =. `name = value` is not an assignment: Bash runs a command called name with the arguments = and value. Names contain letters, digits and underscores and cannot start with a digit. Use lowercase for your own variables so they never collide with environment and shell variables, which are conventionally uppercase.

All Bash variables hold strings unless you give them an attribute. The value on the right of = undergoes expansion but not word splitting or globbing, so `files=$list` is safe without quotes — but quoting it anyway costs nothing and keeps habits consistent.

$name and ${name} read a value. Braces are required when the name is followed by characters that could continue it: "${base}_backup" versus "$base_backup", which reads a different, probably unset, variable. Reading an unset variable yields an empty string unless set -u is active.

unset name removes a variable. readonly name (or declare -r) prevents later assignment or unsetting for the rest of the shell. declare -i makes assignments evaluate as arithmetic, and declare -l / -u fold assigned values to lower or upper case. declare -p name prints a variable together with its attributes in re-usable form, the best way to inspect one.

Attributes are convenient but invisible at the point of use: with declare -i n, the assignment n=2+3 stores 5, surprising anyone who did not see the declaration. Prefer explicit arithmetic $(( )) for clarity and reserve attributes for constants (readonly) and case normalization.
code:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
base=report
echo "${base}_2026.txt"
echo "[$base_2026]"
declare -i total=2+3
declare -u shout=quiet
readonly version=1.0
declare -p total shout version
(version=2.0) 2>/dev/null || echo 'readonly assignment failed'
unset base
echo "base is now [${base}]"
challenge: Declare a lowercase-folding variable named answer, assign it the value YES, and print it. Then print its declaration with declare -p.
solution:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
declare -l answer
answer=YES
echo "$answer"
declare -p answer
question: What does `count = 1` do in Bash?
correct: Runs a command named count with arguments = and 1
wrong: Raises a syntax error before running
reasoning: Assignments must have no spaces around =; otherwise the first word is a command name.
expectedStdout:
report_2026.txt
[]
declare -i total="5"
declare -u shout="QUIET"
declare -r version="1.0"
readonly assignment failed
base is now []

title: Shell variables, the environment and export
body: A shell variable lives only inside the current shell. The environment is a separate list of name=value strings that the kernel copies into every new process. export name marks a shell variable so that it is placed into the environment of commands Bash starts from then on.

Children receive a copy. A child process can change its copy, but nothing it does can flow back to the parent. This is the single most important fact about environment variables, and it is why a script cannot set variables in your interactive shell unless you source it.

A prefix assignment such as `LC_ALL=C sort file` exports a value into one command's environment only. It does not change the shell variable afterwards. This is the cleanest way to configure a single program.

Subshells — ( ... ), command substitutions and pipeline parts — are copies of the shell itself, so they see all shell variables, exported or not. That differs from external programs, which only see exported ones. Confusing these two cases is common: `x=1; bash -c 'echo $x'` prints nothing, but `( echo $x )` prints 1.

export -n removes the export mark; env prints the environment; env -i runs a command with an empty environment, which is how this guide tests every script. declare -x is equivalent to export and also works inside functions together with local.
code:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# shellcheck disable=SC2016  # the inner script must expand $plain itself
plain=one
exported=two
export exported
bash -c 'echo "child sees: [$plain] [$exported]"'
( echo "subshell sees: [$plain] [$exported]" )
GREETING=hi bash -c 'echo "prefix: $GREETING"'
echo "after prefix: [${GREETING-unset}]"
exported=changed bash -c 'exported=child-only'
echo "parent still has: $exported"
challenge: Write a script that exports MODE=test, then runs a child bash that prints MODE and changes it to prod, and finally prints MODE in the parent, demonstrating that the parent value is unchanged.
solution:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# shellcheck disable=SC2016  # the child shell expands $MODE
export MODE=test
bash -c 'echo "child: $MODE"; MODE=prod; echo "child now: $MODE"'
echo "parent: $MODE"
question: Which commands can see a non-exported shell variable?
correct: Subshells of the same shell, but not separately executed programs
wrong: No other command, not even subshells
reasoning: Subshells are copies of the shell and inherit all variables; external programs receive only the exported environment.
expectedStdout:
child sees: [] [two]
subshell sees: [one] [two]
prefix: hi
after prefix: [unset]
parent still has: two
solutionStdout:
child: test
child now: prod
parent: test

title: Defaults, required values and alternatives
body: Parameter expansion can supply fallbacks without an if statement. ${v:-word} expands to word when v is unset or empty, otherwise to $v. ${v:=word} does the same and also assigns word to v. ${v:+word} expands to word only when v is set and non-empty, otherwise to nothing. ${v:?message} prints message and exits a non-interactive shell when v is unset or empty.

Removing the colon changes the test from "unset or empty" to "unset only": ${v-word} keeps an explicitly empty value. Choose deliberately — an empty string passed by a user may be meaningful or may be a mistake.

The common pattern for configuration is `: "${PORT:=8080}"`. The colon builtin does nothing, but its argument is expanded, so the assignment happens. Quote it so that a value with spaces or glob characters is not split or expanded as a pattern.

${1:?usage: script FILE} is a compact way to require an argument, and its message goes to stderr. For user-facing tools, an explicit check with a helpful usage function is friendlier, but :? is excellent for internal invariants.

${v:+word} is handy for optional flags: `cmd ${verbose:+--verbose}` adds the flag only when verbose is non-empty. Because the result must vanish when empty, this is one of the few places where an unquoted expansion is intentional; with arrays you can avoid even that.
code:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
unset name
empty=''
echo "1: ${name:-guest} ${empty:-fallback} ${empty-kept-empty}"
: "${port:=8080}"
echo "2: port=$port"
verbose=1
echo "3: [${verbose:+--verbose}] [${name:+--name}]"
( : "${name:?name is required}" ) 2>&1
echo "4: status $?"
challenge: Write a script that requires a first argument with ${1:?...} and uses ${2:-out.txt} as a default output name. Call it as a function main with the single argument data.csv, printing "data.csv -> out.txt".
question: How do ${v:-x} and ${v-x} differ?
correct: The colon form also substitutes x when v is set but empty
wrong: The colon form exits on error
reasoning: With the colon, both unset and empty trigger the default; without it, only unset does.
expectedStdout:
1: guest fallback 
2: port=8080

../main.sh: line 9: name: name is required
4: status 1

title: Trimming, slicing, replacing and case
body: ${#v} is the length in characters. ${v:offset} and ${v:offset:length} take substrings; a negative offset counts from the end but must be separated from the colon by a space or parentheses (${v: -3}), otherwise it is read as the :- default operator.

${v#pattern} removes the shortest match of pattern from the start and ${v##pattern} the longest; % and %% do the same from the end. With glob patterns these replace many uses of basename, dirname and sed: ${path##*/} is the file name, ${path%/*} the directory, ${file%.*} drops the last extension.

${v/pattern/replacement} replaces the first match and ${v//pattern/replacement} every match. Anchor with /# (start) or /% (end). In Bash 5.2 and later, an unquoted & in the replacement stands for the matched text (the patsub_replacement option); quote the replacement or escape & when you mean a literal ampersand.

Case conversion: ${v^} uppercases the first character, ${v^^} the whole value, and ${v,} / ${v,,} lowercase. Transformations with @ add more: ${v@Q} quotes for reuse, ${v@U}/${v@L} change case, ${v@a} prints attributes, ${v@E} expands backslash escapes.

These operations run inside the shell without starting a process, which matters in loops over thousands of lines. Patterns here are glob patterns, not regular expressions; use [[ =~ ]] when you need a regex.
code:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
path=/var/log/app/server.log.gz
echo "${#path} chars"
echo "file: ${path##*/}  dir: ${path%/*}"
echo "stem: ${path%%.*}  minus last ext: ${path%.*}"
echo "last 2: ${path: -2}  slice: ${path:5:3}"
name='hello world'
echo "${name^} | ${name^^} | ${name// /_}"
echo "${name/#hello/bye} | ${name/%world/there}"
echo "${name/world/[&]}"
printf '%s\n' "${name@Q}"
challenge: Given file="Holiday Photo.JPEG", print it with spaces replaced by dashes, all lowercase, and the extension changed to .jpg: holiday-photo.jpg.
question: Why must a negative offset be written ${v: -3} with a space?
correct: Without the space, :- is the use-default operator
wrong: It is only a style rule
reasoning: ${v:-3} means "v or 3 if unset or empty", so the space (or parentheses) distinguishes a substring offset.
expectedStdout:
26 chars
file: server.log.gz  dir: /var/log/app
stem: /var/log/app/server  minus last ext: /var/log/app/server.log
last 2: gz  slice: log
Hello world | HELLO WORLD | hello_world
bye world | hello there
hello [world]
'hello world'

title: Indirection and name references
body: Sometimes the name of a variable is itself data. ${!name} expands to the value of the variable whose name is stored in name. ${!prefix@} lists the names of all variables starting with prefix, useful for collecting related configuration.

declare -n ref=target creates a name reference: every read or write of ref acts on target. Inside a function, `local -n out=$1` lets the caller pass the name of a variable or array to fill — Bash's way of returning more than a status and a stream of text.

Namerefs have a sharp edge: if the function's own local variable has the same name as the caller's variable, the reference points to the local one (a circular or shadowed reference). Give nameref and local variables distinctive names, such as a leading underscore, in library functions.

ShellCheck cannot see writes made through ${!name} or a nameref, so it may report SC2034 (assigned but unused) or SC2154 (used but never assigned). Silence those with a disable directive and a comment saying why, rather than restructuring correct code. Never let untrusted input choose a variable name: a name like a[$(command)] can execute code when it is expanded. Validate names against a strict pattern such as ^[A-Za-z_][A-Za-z0-9_]*$ before using them indirectly.
Indirection is a power tool. Associative arrays (stage 6) are usually a clearer way to store key/value data than many variables with computed names.
code:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# shellcheck disable=SC2034,SC2154  # ShellCheck cannot follow indirect or nameref access
cfg_host=example.org
cfg_port=443
key=cfg_host
echo "${key} = ${!key}"
for name in "${!cfg_@}"; do
    echo "$name=${!name}"
done
set_result() {
    local -n _out=$1
    _out="computed in ${FUNCNAME[0]}"
}
set_result answer
echo "$answer"
challenge: Write a function split_pair that takes a "key=value" string and the names of two variables, and assigns the key and value to them through namerefs. Call it with "lang=bash", k and v, then print "k=lang v=bash".
question: What does `local -n out=$1` give a function?
correct: A reference through which it reads and writes the caller-named variable
wrong: A copy of the caller variable
The output of the command named by $1
reasoning: A nameref aliases another variable by name, letting functions return results into variables the caller chooses.

cfg_port=443
computed in set_result

title: Positional and special parameters
body: $1 to $9 are the first positional parameters; from the tenth on you need braces: ${10}. $# is how many there are and $0 is the script or shell name. set -- a b c replaces the positional parameters, and shift N drops the first N.

"$@" expands to every positional parameter as a separate word, preserving empty strings and spaces exactly. "$*" joins them into one word with the first character of IFS. Unquoted $@ and $* both undergo word splitting and globbing and are almost always bugs. When forwarding arguments, write "$@".

$? is the exit status of the last foreground command and changes after every command — save it immediately (rc=$?) if you need it later. $$ is the process ID of the main shell (it does not change in subshells; $BASHPID does). $! is the PID of the most recent background job.
$- lists the active single-letter options (e.g. h, B, and e when errexit is on). $_ is the last argument of the previous command, handy interactively but fragile in scripts.
Bash-specific arrays describe the call stack: FUNCNAME, BASH_SOURCE and BASH_LINENO. These are the basis for useful error messages and are covered in the debugging lessons.
code:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -- 'first arg' '' third
echo "count: $#"
printf '@[%s]\n' "$@"
printf '*[%s]\n' "$*"
set -- {a..l}
echo "tenth: ${10}  ninth: $9"
shift 10
echo "after shift: $* ($#)"
false
rc=$?
echo "saved status: $rc, now: $?"
( [[ $$ == "$BASHPID" ]] || echo 'subshell: $$ kept, BASHPID changed' )
challenge: Write a function count_args that prints how many arguments it received and then each one in brackets. Call it with "$@" after setting the parameters to: one "two words" "" (an empty string). It should report 3.
question: How should a wrapper forward all of its arguments unchanged?
reasoning: Only quoted "$@" keeps each argument as its own word, including empty ones and ones with spaces.

@[]

title: Glob patterns and pathname expansion
body: An unquoted word containing *, ? or [ is a pattern. During pathname expansion Bash replaces it with the sorted list of matching file names. * matches any string including the empty one, ? exactly one character, and [abc] one character from the set; [a-z] is a range and [!abc] or [^abc] negates the set.

POSIX character classes work inside brackets: [[:digit:]], [[:alpha:]], [[:space:]], [[:upper:]]. They are locale-aware and clearer than ranges, whose meaning can change between locales — [a-z] may include uppercase letters in some locales unless the globasciiranges option (on by default since Bash 5.0) applies.

Globs match against names in a directory, not file contents, and they never cross a slash: */*.txt matches .txt files one level down. A leading dot must be matched explicitly, so * skips hidden files such as .env unless dotglob is set. . and .. are never matched by * .

When nothing matches, Bash by default leaves the pattern unchanged as a literal word. A loop `for f in *.log` with no log files therefore runs once with f set to the string *.log — a frequent cause of "No such file" errors. The next lesson shows nullglob and failglob, which fix this.

The same pattern syntax appears in case statements, [[ $x == pattern ]], and the trimming expansions ${v#pattern}. In those places nothing is matched against the filesystem; the pattern is tested against a string. Quote any part you want to be literal: [[ $x == "*" ]] tests for a literal star.
code:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
touch report1.txt report2.txt report10.txt notes.md .hidden
printf '%s ' *.txt; echo
printf '%s ' report?.txt; echo
printf '%s ' report[[:digit:]][[:digit:]].txt; echo
printf '%s ' [!r]*; echo
for f in *.log; do echo "unmatched pattern stays literal: $f"; done
name='*.txt'
# shellcheck disable=SC2053  # unquoted on purpose: the value is used as a pattern
[[ report1.txt == $name ]] && echo 'string matched as pattern'
[[ report1.txt == "$name" ]] || echo 'quoted pattern is literal'

question: What happens to `*.log` in a command when no file matches, with default options?
correct: The pattern is passed unchanged as a literal word
reasoning: Without nullglob or failglob, an unmatched glob stays literal, so loops run once with the pattern itself.

report1.txt report2.txt 
report10.txt

string matched as pattern

title: nullglob, failglob, dotglob and globstar
body: shopt -s nullglob makes a pattern with no matches expand to nothing. Loops over *.log then run zero times, and arrays like files=(*.log) are empty when there is nothing to process — the behaviour most scripts want.

shopt -s failglob instead makes an unmatched pattern an error: the command is not run. This is stricter and surfaces missing inputs early. Be careful with nullglob in commands like `ls *.log`: with no matches, ls receives no arguments and lists the whole directory.

dotglob lets * match names that start with a dot (still never . or ..). nocaseglob makes matching case-insensitive. globstar enables **, which matches any number of directories when it is a whole path component: **/*.txt finds text files at every depth, including the top level.

shopt -s enables and shopt -u disables an option; shopt -q name tests it silently. Options are shell state, so enable them near the top of a script, or inside a subshell or function where you restore them, rather than toggling them in scattered places.

globstar walks the tree in the shell and follows no symbolic links to directories since Bash 4.3. For very large trees or when you need filtering by type, size or time, find is still the right tool; combine them by using find -print0 with read -d '' (stage 8).
code:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
mkdir -p src/lib/deep
touch top.txt src/a.txt src/lib/deep/b.txt .secret.txt
files=(*.log)
echo "default: ${#files[@]} element(s): ${files[*]}"
shopt -s nullglob
files=(*.log)
echo "nullglob: ${#files[@]} element(s)"
shopt -s globstar dotglob
printf '%s\n' **/*.txt
shopt -u dotglob
( shopt -s failglob; echo *.missing ) 2>&1 | sed 's/^.*line [0-9]*: //'

correct: nullglob
reasoning: nullglob removes unmatched patterns; failglob turns them into errors; dotglob and extglob change what can match.

title: Extended globs
body: With shopt -s extglob Bash adds pattern operators that resemble a small regular-expression language: ?(list) matches zero or one occurrence, *(list) zero or more, +(list) one or more, @(list) exactly one of the alternatives, and !(list) anything except the alternatives. list is one or more patterns separated by |.
!(*.jpg|*.png) selects every file that is not an image — something plain globs cannot express. @(start|stop|restart) checks a word against a fixed set, and +([[:digit:]]) means "one or more digits".

Extended patterns also work in [[ == ]], case and parameter expansions. Since Bash 5.2 extglob is enabled automatically inside [[ ]] pattern matching, but it must be turned on with shopt for filename expansion and other uses. Enable it on its own line before the code that uses it: the option affects parsing, so turning it on inside the same compound command or function definition that uses the pattern is too late.
*( ) patterns can be slow on long strings because matching may backtrack heavily. Use them for names and short words, and [[ =~ ]] or external tools for large text processing.
Trimming with extended patterns is a neat trick: ${s##*( )} removes all leading spaces, where plain ${s##* } would remove everything up to the last space.
code:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
shopt -s extglob
touch photo.jpg logo.png notes.txt data.csv
printf '%s ' !(*.jpg|*.png); echo
for word in start stop pause; do
    [[ $word == @(start|stop|restart) ]] && echo "$word: valid action" || echo "$word: unknown"
done
for id in 42 4x2 ''; do
    [[ $id == +([[:digit:]]) ]] && echo "[$id] numeric" || echo "[$id] not numeric"
done
s='    indented text'
echo "[${s##*( )}]"

question: What does !(*.txt) match when extglob is enabled?
correct: Every name that does not match *.txt
wrong: Only names containing an exclamation mark
reasoning: !(pattern-list) matches anything except the listed patterns.

stop: valid action
pause: unknown
[42] numeric
[4x2] not numeric
[] not numeric

title: Brace expansion
body: Brace expansion generates words, whether or not any files exist. a{b,c,d}e becomes abe ace ade. A sequence {1..5} counts, {a..e} steps through letters, {10..0..2} counts down by two, and leading zeros pad every item: {01..10}.
It is the first expansion performed and is purely textual, which is why variables cannot appear inside a sequence. For dynamic ranges use a C-style for loop: for ((i = 1; i <= n; i++)).
Braces are not expanded when quoted, and a single item without a comma, such as {x}, stays literal. Expansions nest and combine: {a,b}{1,2} produces a1 a2 b1 b2.

Practical uses: mkdir -p project/{src,tests,docs}, cp file{,.bak} to make file.bak, and mv name.{txt,md} to rename an extension. The words generated are then subject to the later expansions, so mixing braces with globs works.
Brace expansion is a Bash (and ksh/zsh) feature, not POSIX sh. In a #!/bin/sh script it may be passed through literally, which is one reason to choose your shebang deliberately.
challenge: Use one brace expansion to create the directories logs/2026-01 through logs/2026-03, then print their names one per line.
question: Why does mkdir {1..$n} create a directory literally named {1..3} when n=3?
correct: Brace expansion happens before the variable is expanded
reasoning: Brace expansion is first and textual; it sees $n literally and cannot form a range.
expectedStdout:
fileA.txt fileB.txt fileC.txt
1 2 3 4 5 a b c d e 10 8 6 4 2 0
01 04 07 10
project/docs project/src project/tests 
app.conf app.conf.bak 
a1 a2 b1 b2 {not,expanded}

title: Sorting glob results with GLOBSORT (Bash 5.3)
body: Bash 5.3 adds the GLOBSORT variable, which controls how pathname-expansion results are ordered. Unset or empty keeps the historical behaviour: ascending by name according to the locale collation order.

A value is an optional + or - (descending) followed by a key: name, numeric, size, mtime, atime, ctime or blocks. -mtime lists the newest files first; size lists the smallest first. When two files compare equal, the name breaks the tie, so results are deterministic.

numeric treats names made entirely of digits as numbers, so 2 sorts before 10. Names containing non-digits sort after all-digit names using the normal name order — so it does not perform "natural sort" on names like file10.
nosort returns names in the order the directory provides them, which can be faster for huge directories when order does not matter, but it is filesystem-dependent and not stable across machines.
GLOBSORT is ignored by older shells: macOS /bin/bash 3.2 simply sorts by name. If a script relies on the order, require Bash 5.3 explicitly (check BASH_VERSINFO) or fall back to an external sort.
code:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
printf '%0100d' 0 > big.txt
printf 'ab' > small.txt
printf 'abcd' > mid.txt
touch 1 2 10
GLOBSORT=size
echo *.txt
GLOBSORT=-size
echo *.txt
GLOBSORT=numeric
echo [0-9]*
GLOBSORT=
echo [0-9]*

correct: 2, 10, then file1
reasoning: All-digit names sort by numeric value first; names with other characters come afterwards in name order.

title: Exit status: success, failure and conventions
body: Every command returns an integer from 0 to 255. Zero means success; anything else means failure, and programs document what the non-zero values mean. grep returns 0 when it finds a match, 1 when it finds none and 2 for an error such as an unreadable file — "no match" and "error" are different failures.

Bash reserves some values. 126 means the command was found but could not be executed; 127 means it was not found; 128+N means the command was killed by signal N (130 after Ctrl-C, which is SIGINT 2; 143 after SIGTERM 15). exit 256 wraps to 0, so keep explicit statuses between 0 and 125.

$? holds the status of the most recent command and is overwritten by the very next one, including echo and [[. Capture it immediately with rc=$? when you need to inspect it, or better, test the command directly in an if.

! command inverts a status: success becomes 1 and failure becomes 0. A pipeline's status is that of its last command unless pipefail is set (stage 9). true and false are commands that only return 0 and 1.
Scripts should end with a meaningful status: 0 when they did their job, non-zero with a message on stderr otherwise. Callers, CI systems and && chains rely on it.
code:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
printf 'apple\nbanana\n' > fruit.txt
grep -q banana fruit.txt; echo "match: $?"
grep -q cherry fruit.txt; echo "no match: $?"
grep -q x missing.txt 2>/dev/null; echo "error: $?"
nosuchcommand 2>/dev/null; echo "not found: $?"
! grep -q cherry fruit.txt && echo 'negated: cherry is absent'
# shellcheck disable=SC2242  # 300 shows the 8-bit wrap on purpose
( exit 300 ); echo "300 wraps to: $?"
bash -c 'kill -TERM $$'; echo "killed by SIGTERM: $?"

question: What exit status does Bash report for a command killed by SIGINT (signal 2)?
reasoning: Death by signal N is reported as 128+N, so SIGINT gives 130.

no match: 1
error: 2

title: if, test, [ ] and [[ ]]
body: if runs a command and branches on its exit status: if cmd; then ...; elif other; then ...; else ...; fi. The condition is any command — `if grep -q x file` is more direct than running grep and checking $? afterwards.

test and its alias [ are ordinary builtins, so their arguments go through word splitting and globbing; always quote variables inside [ ]. The closing ] is just the last argument. [[ ]] is a keyword: it parses its contents specially, does not split or glob variables, supports && || ( ) inside, and adds pattern (==) and regex (=~) matching. In Bash scripts, prefer [[ ]].

String tests: -z s (empty), -n s (non-empty), s1 == s2, s1 != s2, and s1 < s2 for sorting order inside [[ ]]. Numeric tests use -eq -ne -lt -le -gt -ge, or arithmetic (( )) which reads better. Do not use < for numbers inside [[ ]] — it compares strings, so [[ 10 < 9 ]] is true.
File tests: -e exists, -f regular file, -d directory, -L symlink, -s non-empty, -r/-w/-x permissions, f1 -nt f2 newer than. A missing file is not an error for these tests; they simply fail.
The right side of == in [[ ]] is a pattern unless quoted. That is useful ([[ $f == *.txt ]]) but means [[ $a == $b ]] compares a against b as a pattern; write "$b" for an exact comparison.
code:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
mkdir -p data
echo 42 > data/answer.txt
for path in data data/answer.txt data/missing; do
    if [[ -d $path ]]; then echo "$path: directory"
    elif [[ -f $path && -s $path ]]; then echo "$path: non-empty file"
    else echo "$path: missing"
    fi
done
value=''
[ -z "$value" ] && echo '[ ] with quotes: empty'
# shellcheck disable=SC2071,SC2050  # the string-comparison pitfall is the lesson
[[ 10 < 9 ]] && echo '[[ 10 < 9 ]] is a string comparison: true'
(( 10 > 9 )) && echo '(( 10 > 9 )) is numeric: true'
file=notes.txt
[[ $file == *.txt ]] && echo 'pattern match on *.txt'

solution:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
check_age() {
    if [[ ! $1 =~ ^[0-9]+$ ]]; then
        echo invalid
    elif (( $1 < 18 )); then
        echo minor
    else
        echo adult
    fi
}
for age in 15 30 2x; do check_age "$age"; done

correct: < inside [[ ]] compares strings lexicographically
reasoning: Use -lt or (( )) for numbers; inside [[ ]], < and > compare strings.

data/missing: missing

title: Regular expressions with =~ and BASH_REMATCH
body: [[ string =~ regex ]] matches using POSIX extended regular expressions. On success, BASH_REMATCH[0] holds the whole match and BASH_REMATCH[1], [2]... the parenthesized groups. On failure the array is cleared.

The regex is unanchored: it matches anywhere unless you use ^ and $. Quoted parts of the right-hand side are matched literally, which is why the reliable style is to store the regex in a variable and write [[ $s =~ $re ]] unquoted.

POSIX ERE has no \d, lazy quantifiers or lookarounds; use [0-9] or [[:digit:]]. Matching is greedy. Bracket ranges are locale-dependent; in scripts that must be predictable, set LC_ALL=C or use character classes.

An invalid regex makes the test return 2, distinguishing a broken pattern from a non-match (status 1); Bash 5.3 also prints an error message naming the problem. Always handle status 2 when the pattern comes from configuration or users.
For extracting several fields from structured lines, =~ with groups is clean and avoids external processes. For processing whole files, awk or grep -E are usually faster than a Bash loop.
code:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
re='^([a-z]+)-([0-9]+)\.([a-z]+)$'
for name in app-42.log notes.txt server-7.gz; do
    if [[ $name =~ $re ]]; then
        echo "$name -> base=${BASH_REMATCH[1]} n=${BASH_REMATCH[2]} ext=${BASH_REMATCH[3]}"
    else
        echo "$name -> no match"
    fi
done
# shellcheck disable=SC2050,SC2076  # constant operands show literal versus regex matching
[[ a.c =~ a.c && abc =~ a.c ]] && echo 'unquoted dot matches any char'
# shellcheck disable=SC2050,SC2076
[[ abc =~ "a.c" ]] || echo 'quoted dot is literal'
bad='('
[[ x =~ $bad ]] 2>/dev/null; echo "invalid regex status: $?"

correct: Quoted parts of the right side are matched literally, so an unquoted variable keeps regex meaning without escaping problems
reasoning: Quoting the right-hand side turns regex characters into literals; [[ $s =~ $re ]] keeps them as regex syntax.

notes.txt -> no match

title: Integer arithmetic with $(( )) and (( ))
body: $(( expression )) expands to the result of integer arithmetic; (( expression )) evaluates it as a command whose status is 0 when the result is non-zero and 1 when it is zero. Inside, variables do not need $, and C operators work: + - * / % ** ++ -- += << >> & | ^ ~, comparisons, && ||, and the ternary a ? b : c.

Arithmetic is 64-bit signed integer. Division truncates toward zero, % keeps the sign of the dividend, and overflow wraps silently. Bash has no floating point: $(( 7 / 2 )) is 3. Use awk or bc for decimals, or scale integers yourself (work in cents, not euros). Bash 5.3 also ships an optional fltexpr loadable builtin for floating-point expressions.
Numbers with leading zeros are octal: $(( 08 )) is an error and $(( 010 )) is 8. When values come from dates or user input, force base 10 with 10#$value. Other bases use base#digits: 16#ff, 2#1010.

A trap with (( )): when the expression evaluates to 0 the status is 1. (( count++ )) with count=0 therefore "fails", which stops a script running under set -e. Prefer count=$((count + 1)) or (( ++count )) when errexit is active.

Never put untrusted text into arithmetic. Arithmetic evaluation expands array subscripts, so input like a[$(cmd)] can execute commands. Validate that input is numeric with [[ $x =~ ^-?[0-9]+$ ]] first.

#!/usr/bin/env bash

echo "hex ff=$((16#ff)) binary 1010=$((2#1010)) octal 010=$((010))"
day=09
echo "day+1 = $((10#$day + 1))"
count=0
(( count++ )) || echo "(( count++ )) returned status 1 because the old value was 0"
echo "max int: $(( (1 << 63) - 1 ))"

title: case: matching words against patterns
body: case word in pattern) commands ;; ... esac compares one word against glob patterns from top to bottom and runs the first matching branch. Patterns can list alternatives with |, and *) is the conventional catch-all at the end.

case is the idiomatic way to dispatch on subcommands, options and file extensions. It does not split or glob the word, so `case $1 in` is safe without quotes; patterns themselves are globs unless quoted.
Branch terminators: ;; stops; ;& falls through into the next branch's commands without testing its pattern; ;;& continues testing the following patterns and may run several branches.
case is POSIX and works in every shell, so it is also the portable replacement for [[ == pattern ]] in /bin/sh scripts.
Keep each branch short. When a branch grows, call a function, so the dispatch table stays readable at a glance.

title: for, while, until, break and continue
body: for name in words; do ...; done iterates over a list after expansion. Iterate over "$@" or "${array[@]}" to keep items intact; iterating over $(command) splits on whitespace and globs, which breaks on file names with spaces.
The C-style loop for (( i = 0; i < n; i++ )) counts with arithmetic and accepts variables, unlike brace ranges. while cmd runs as long as cmd succeeds and until cmd as long as it fails.

Reading input line by line uses while IFS= read -r line; do ...; done < file. The redirect belongs after done, so the whole loop reads from the file. If the last line has no trailing newline, read returns failure but still fills line; `|| [[ -n $line ]]` processes it too.
break leaves the innermost loop and continue skips to its next iteration; break 2 and continue 2 act on the enclosing loop. Prefer a function with return when the control flow becomes deep.

A loop fed by a pipe (cmd | while read ...) runs in a subshell, so variables set inside it are lost afterwards. Use redirection from a file, process substitution < <(cmd), or shopt -s lastpipe (stage 9) to keep them.
code:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
for fruit in 'green apple' pear; do echo "fruit: $fruit"; done
n=3
for (( i = 1; i <= n; i++ )); do printf '%d ' "$i"; done; echo
printf 'alpha\nbeta\ngamma' > words.txt
count=0
while IFS= read -r word || [[ -n $word ]]; do
    (( ++count ))
    [[ $word == beta ]] && continue
    echo "word $count: $word"
done < words.txt
for x in 1 2 3; do
    for y in a b c; do
        [[ $y == b ]] && continue 2
        echo "$x$y"
    done
done
until (( n == 0 )); do (( n-- )); done; echo "n=$n"

title: Indexed arrays
body: An indexed array holds a list of strings addressed by integer subscripts from 0. Create one with a=(one "two words" three), append with a+=(four), and assign one element with a[5]=six. ${a[1]} reads one element; without a subscript, $a means ${a[0]}, a common source of bugs.

"${a[@]}" expands to every element as a separate word — the array equivalent of "$@" — and is the form to use almost everywhere. "${a[*]}" joins elements with the first IFS character into one word. ${#a[@]} counts elements and ${#a[1]} is the length of one element.

Arrays may be sparse: unset 'a[1]' removes an element without renumbering the rest. ${!a[@]} lists the indices that exist, which is how you iterate safely over a sparse array. Quote the argument to unset so that the brackets are not treated as a glob.
Slices use ${a[@]:start:count}; negative subscripts count from the end: ${a[-1]} is the last element. Since slices follow the order of existing indices, they work on sparse arrays too.
Arrays cannot be exported to child processes and cannot be nested. To pass a list to another program, pass it as arguments ("${a[@]}") or write it NUL-separated to a pipe or file.
code:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
fruits=(apple 'green pear' cherry)
fruits+=(date)
echo "count: ${#fruits[@]}, first: ${fruits[0]}, last: ${fruits[-1]}"
printf '[%s] ' "${fruits[@]}"; echo
printf '[%s] ' "${fruits[*]}"; echo
printf '[%s] ' "${fruits[@]:1:2}"; echo
unset 'fruits[1]'
echo "indices now: ${!fruits[*]}"
for i in "${!fruits[@]}"; do echo "$i=${fruits[i]}"; done

reversed=()
for (( i = ${#words[@]} - 1; i >= 0; i-- )); do
    reversed+=("${words[i]}")
done
echo "${reversed[*]}"

correct: The element at index 0
reasoning: A bare array name refers to element 0; use "${arr[@]}" for all elements.

title: Associative arrays (maps)
body: declare -A creates an associative array keyed by strings: declare -A port=([http]=80 [https]=443). The declaration is mandatory — assigning m[key]=v without it creates an indexed array and evaluates key as arithmetic. Inside functions, local -A creates a local map.
${!m[@]} lists the keys and "${m[@]}" the values. Their order is unspecified, so sort the keys whenever output order matters: printf '%s\n' "${!m[@]}" | sort, or a loop over a sorted key list.
Test whether a key exists with [[ -v m[$key] ]]; testing [[ -n ${m[$key]} ]] cannot tell a missing key from an empty value. unset 'm[key]' removes one entry and unset m the whole map.
Counting is the classic use: (( count[$word]++ )) or count[$word]=$(( ${count[$word]:-0} + 1 )). Remember that (( )) returns status 1 when the old value is 0 if you run under set -e.
Associative arrays need Bash 4 or later — the macOS /bin/bash 3.2 rejects declare -A. Requiring a modern Bash, or failing early with a clear message, is better than failing halfway through.
code:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
declare -A port=([http]=80 [https]=443)
port[ssh]=22
echo "https -> ${port[https]} (${#port[@]} entries)"
while IFS= read -r name; do
    echo "$name=${port[$name]}"
done < <(printf '%s\n' "${!port[@]}" | sort)
[[ -v port[ftp] ]] || echo 'no ftp entry'
declare -A count=()
for word in to be or not to be; do
    count[$word]=$(( ${count[$word]:-0} + 1 ))
done
for word in be not or to; do echo "$word: ${count[$word]}"; done

    team[$group]+="${team[$group]:+,}$person"

    echo "$group: ${team[$group]}"
done < <(printf '%s\n' "${!team[@]}" | sort)

title: Reading lines into arrays with mapfile
body: mapfile (also called readarray) reads lines from standard input into an indexed array, one element per line. -t removes the trailing newline from each element; you almost always want it. mapfile -t lines < file is far faster than a while-read loop that appends.

-d delim changes the line terminator. mapfile -d '' reads NUL-terminated records, which pairs perfectly with find -print0 or printf '%s\0' and is the only fully safe way to handle file names that may contain newlines.

-n count limits how many lines are read, -s count skips leading lines (for a header) and -O origin starts at a given index. -C callback with -c quantum runs a function every N lines, useful for progress reporting.
Feed command output with process substitution: mapfile -t items < <(command). Do not write command | mapfile -t items: mapfile would run in a subshell and the array would vanish.
mapfile keeps empty lines as empty elements, unlike splitting with read -a or an unquoted $(...).
code:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
printf 'name,score\nada,95\n\nalan,88\n' > scores.csv
mapfile -t -s 1 rows < scores.csv
echo "${#rows[@]} rows after the header (one is empty)"
printf '[%s]\n' "${rows[@]}"
touch 'plain.txt' $'odd\nname.txt'
mapfile -d '' -t files < <(find . -name '*.txt' -print0 | sort -z)
echo "${#files[@]} files"
printf '%q\n' "${files[@]}"

title: Building command lines with arrays
body: Arrays are the correct way to build a command whose arguments vary. Put the command and its arguments in an array, add options conditionally, and run it with "${cmd[@]}". Every element stays exactly one argument, whatever it contains.

The tempting alternative — building a string and running it unquoted, or with eval — breaks on spaces and quotes and invites code injection. BashFAQ 50, "I'm trying to put a command in a variable", exists because this mistake is so common.

Optional arguments: start with args=() and append with args+=(--verbose) inside an if. For printing the command for a log, use printf '%q ' "${cmd[@]}" so the logged line can be pasted back into a shell.

Filtering and de-duplicating: loop and append the elements you keep; use an associative array as a "seen" set to drop duplicates while keeping the original order. Sorting goes through an external sort with NUL delimiters and mapfile.
Functions can return arrays through a nameref (local -n) or by printing NUL-separated values that the caller reads with mapfile -d ''.
code:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
show() { printf '<%s> ' "$@"; echo; }
verbose=1
pattern='two words'
args=(--count)
(( verbose )) && args+=(--verbose)
args+=(-- "$pattern" 'my file.txt')
show "${args[@]}"
printf '%q ' grep "${args[@]}"; echo
declare -A seen=()
unique=()
for item in b a b c a; do
    [[ -v seen[$item] ]] && continue
    seen[$item]=1
    unique+=("$item")
done
echo "unique in order: ${unique[*]}"
mapfile -d '' -t sorted < <(printf '%s\0' "${unique[@]}" | sort -rz)
echo "sorted desc: ${sorted[*]}"

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# shellcheck disable=SC2154  # kept is filled through the nameref
only_long() {
    local -n _result=$1
    local min=$2 word
    shift 2
    _result=()
    for word in "$@"; do
        (( ${#word} >= min )) && _result+=("$word")
    done
    return 0
}

title: Safe subscripts with array_expand_once (Bash 5.3)
body: Some builtins evaluate an array subscript a second time. With an attacker-controlled key such as $(command), test -v "m[$key]", printf -v "m[$key]", unset "m[$key]" and read into "m[$key]" can run the embedded command substitution: the first expansion produces the text, and the builtin then expands the subscript again.

Bash 5.3 adds shopt array_expand_once (replacing the older assoc_expand_once, which is now a deprecated synonym). When set, the shell expands subscripts only once in arithmetic evaluation and in builtins that assign or dereference array elements, so keys are treated purely as data.

Enable it at the top of any script that uses untrusted strings as array keys: shopt -s array_expand_once. The [[ -v m[$key] ]] keyword form is parsed by the shell itself and is already safe; the risk is in the builtins that receive the subscript as a string argument.

Defence in depth still applies: validate keys when you can, prefer keyword tests, and remember that indexed-array subscripts are arithmetic expressions, so arbitrary text should never be used as an indexed subscript at all.
The option is unknown to older Bash versions, so shopt -s array_expand_once fails there. That failure is a useful early signal that the script needs a newer shell.
code:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
declare -A m
# shellcheck disable=SC2016  # the key must stay literal: it simulates hostile input
key='$(echo INJECTED >&2; echo k)'
m[$key]=1
shopt -s array_expand_once
test -v "m[$key]" && echo 'test -v treats the key as data'
printf -v "m[$key]" '%s' 2
echo "printf -v updated it to ${m[$key]}"
unset "m[$key]"
echo "entries left: ${#m[@]}"
challenge: With array_expand_once enabled, count occurrences of three untrusted keys read from a here-document — a, $(id), a — in an associative array using printf -v, then print each key with %q and its count in sorted order.
solution:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
shopt -s array_expand_once
declare -A seen=()
while IFS= read -r key; do
    printf -v "seen[$key]" '%d' $(( ${seen[$key]:-0} + 1 ))
done <<'EOF'
a
$(id)
a
EOF
while IFS= read -r key; do
    printf '%q %s\n' "$key" "${seen[$key]}"
done < <(printf '%s\n' "${!seen[@]}" | sort)

correct: Builtins expanding an array subscript a second time, which can run code hidden in a key
wrong: Slow expansion of very large arrays

title: Defining and calling functions
body: A function is a named compound command: name() { commands; }. The function keyword (function name { ... }) is a Bash alternative; the name() form is portable. Define a function before the line that calls it runs — Bash executes top to bottom, so a common layout is all functions first, then main "$@" at the bottom.

Functions are called exactly like commands and receive their own positional parameters: inside, $1, $2, "$@" and $# refer to the function's arguments, while $0 is still the script name. FUNCNAME[0] is the current function's name.

The body can be any compound command. name() ( ... ) with parentheses runs the body in a subshell every time, which automatically isolates variable changes, cd and shell options — handy for helpers that must not leak state, at the cost of a fork.

A function's exit status is the status of its last command, or the value given to return N. return without a number keeps the last status. exit inside a function ends the whole script, not just the function, which is rarely what a library function should do.
Keep functions small and named for what they do. A good test is whether you can describe a function in one sentence that does not use "and".
challenge: Write a function max that prints the largest of any number of integer arguments, and returns status 1 with no output when called with no arguments. Test it with 3 9 2 and with no arguments, printing the status.

#!/usr/bin/env bash
max() {
    (( $# )) || return 1
    local best=$1 n
    for n in "$@"; do
        (( n > best )) && best=$n
    done
    echo "$best"
}

echo "status: $?"

correct: Ends the entire script (or current shell)
wrong: Nothing unless the function runs in background

title: local variables and dynamic scope
body: Variables are global by default, even when first assigned inside a function. Declare function variables with local (or declare inside a function, which is local by default) so a helper cannot overwrite the caller's variables.

Bash uses dynamic scoping: a local variable is visible to every function called from the function that declared it, for as long as that call is active. A callee that reads or assigns a name sees the nearest one on the call stack, not just globals. This is powerful and surprising; it is why library functions should use local generously and distinctive names.
declare -g inside a function creates or assigns a global even when a local of the same name exists further up the stack — the way to deliberately set global state, for example from an initializer.

local var=$(command) hides the command's failure: the status you get is local's own, which is always 0. Declare first and assign separately — local out; out=$(command) — when you need to check that the command succeeded. ShellCheck reports this as SC2155.
A local array is declared with local -a and a local map with local -A. local - (a single dash) makes shell option changes made with set local to the function, restoring them on return.

title: Returning results from functions
body: A function has three channels back to its caller: the exit status (0–255, meaning success or kind of failure), the text it writes to standard output, and variables it sets. Use each for what it is good at.

Status answers yes/no questions: is_valid "$x" && ... . Output is natural for producing a value: result=$(compute) captures it, but every $(...) forks a subshell, so the function cannot set variables or change directories for the caller, and trailing newlines are stripped.

For several values, or for speed inside loops, write into a variable named by the caller using a nameref, or into an agreed global such as REPLY. Bash itself uses REPLY for read without a name. Document whichever convention you choose.
Errors belong on standard error: echo "error: ..." >&2, followed by a non-zero return. Keeping diagnostics off stdout means $(...) captures only the real result.

Bash 5.3 adds ${ command; } and ${| command; } command substitutions that run in the current shell without forking; stage 9 covers them. They make output capture cheap and let the function set variables too.
code:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
divide() {
    if (( $2 == 0 )); then
        echo 'divide: division by zero' >&2
        return 1
    fi
    echo $(( $1 / $2 ))
}
result=$(divide 10 2) && echo "10/2 = $result"
result=$(divide 1 0 2>&1) || echo "failed with: $result"
minmax() {
    local -n _lo=$1 _hi=$2
    shift 2
    _lo=$1 _hi=$1
    local n
    for n in "$@"; do
        (( n < _lo )) && _lo=$n
        (( n > _hi )) && _hi=$n
    done
    return 0
}

# shellcheck disable=SC2154  # lo and hi are assigned through namerefs
echo "min=$lo max=$hi"

title: Parsing options with getopts
body: getopts is the builtin option parser for short options. getopts 'vo:h' opt reads the next option into opt; a colon after a letter (o:) means it takes an argument, delivered in OPTARG. Loop with while getopts ...; do case $opt in ...; esac; done, then shift $((OPTIND - 1)) to leave only the operands.
It handles the conventional forms automatically: -v -o file, -vo file, -ofile and -- to end options. Bundled flags and attached arguments work without extra code.

Starting the option string with a colon selects silent error reporting: an unknown option sets opt to ? and OPTARG to the letter; a missing argument sets opt to : and OPTARG to the letter. Your case branches can then print helpful messages and exit with status 2, the conventional code for usage errors.

getopts does not understand long options like --output. Common approaches are a hand-written while/case loop over "$@" with shift, or the external GNU getopt (not available in the same form on macOS). Many scripts support both short options via getopts and a few long ones via a pre-pass.
When parsing inside a function, set local OPTIND so repeated calls start fresh; OPTIND is global state otherwise.

title: Libraries, source -p and the main pattern
body: source file (or . file) reads and executes a file in the current shell, so its functions and variables become available. Large scripts split helpers into library files and source them at start-up. Extra arguments after the file name become its positional parameters while it runs.

Locate libraries relative to the script, not the current directory: dir=${BASH_SOURCE[0]%/*} gives the directory of the file being executed, even when it is sourced. BASH_SOURCE is an array that mirrors FUNCNAME, recording which file each stack frame came from.

Bash 5.3 adds source -p PATH: the file is searched for in the colon-separated directories you give instead of in $PATH. This avoids both hard-coded absolute paths and accidental lookups in the user's PATH. Older versions reject the option.

Libraries should only define functions and constants. Guard against double inclusion with a variable such as [[ -v _UTIL_LOADED ]] && return; _UTIL_LOADED=1 — return at the top level of a sourced file stops sourcing it.

Put the program's logic in a main function and finish the file with main "$@". To make a file usable both as a program and as a library, run main only when executed directly: if [[ ${BASH_SOURCE[0]} == "$0" ]]; then main "$@"; fi. Use if rather than the shorter [[ ... ]] && main: when the file is sourced, the && form leaves status 1 as the file's last status, so `source tool.sh && next` would wrongly fail.
code:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
mkdir -p lib
cat > lib/util.sh <<'EOF'
[[ -v _UTIL_LOADED ]] && return
_UTIL_LOADED=1
loads=$(( ${loads:-0} + 1 ))
shout() { echo "${1^^}!"; }
EOF
# shellcheck source=/dev/null
source -p "$PWD/lib" util.sh
# shellcheck source=/dev/null
source -p "$PWD/lib" util.sh
shout hello
# shellcheck disable=SC2154  # loads is set by the sourced library
echo "library body ran $loads time(s)"
cat > tool.sh <<'EOF'
main() { echo "main ran with: $*"; }
if [[ ${BASH_SOURCE[0]} == "$0" ]]; then main "$@"; fi
EOF
bash tool.sh a b
# shellcheck source=/dev/null
source ./tool.sh && echo 'sourced: main not run'
challenge: Create lib/math.sh defining square() (prints n*n), then source it with source -p using a search path containing a nonexistent directory followed by lib, and print square 12.
solution:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
mkdir -p lib
# shellcheck disable=SC2016  # the library text must keep $1 literal
echo 'square() { echo $(( $1 * $1 )); }' > lib/math.sh
# shellcheck source=/dev/null
source -p "$PWD/missing:$PWD/lib" math.sh

question: What does Bash 5.3's source -p PATH change?
correct: The file is searched in the given directories instead of $PATH
wrong: It sources the file in a subshell
It prints each line before running it
It requires the file to be executable
reasoning: source -p takes an explicit colon-separated search path, avoiding dependence on the user's PATH.
expectedStdout:
HELLO!
