main ran with: a b
sourced: main not run

title: File descriptors and redirection
body: Every process starts with three open file descriptors: 0 standard input, 1 standard output and 2 standard error. Redirections rewire them before the command runs: > file truncates and writes stdout to file, >> appends, < file reads stdin from file, and 2> file sends stderr to file. N> and N< apply to any descriptor number.

2>&1 means "make descriptor 2 point where descriptor 1 points right now". Redirections are processed left to right, so order matters: cmd > out 2>&1 sends both streams to out, while cmd 2>&1 > out sends stderr to the original stdout (the terminal) and only stdout to out. &> file is Bash shorthand for > file 2>&1.
/dev/null discards output and supplies empty input. cmd > /dev/null 2>&1 silences a command completely — useful, but be careful not to hide errors you need to see.
set -o noclobber (set -C) makes > refuse to overwrite an existing file; >| overrides it deliberately. It protects against accidental truncation in interactive work and some scripts.

Redirections can appear on compound commands: { ...; } > file, a while loop's done < file, or a function definition, so a whole block shares one redirection — and the file is opened once instead of on every line.
code:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
both() { echo out; echo err >&2; }
both > a.txt 2>&1
printf 'a.txt: %s\n' "$(tr '\n' ' ' < a.txt)"
both 2>&1 > b.txt | sed 's/^/via pipe: /'
printf 'b.txt: %s\n' "$(cat b.txt)"
both &> c.txt; echo "c.txt has $(wc -l < c.txt | tr -d ' ') lines"
echo first > log.txt; echo second >> log.txt; cat log.txt
set -o noclobber
{ echo third > log.txt; } 2>/dev/null || echo 'noclobber refused to overwrite'
echo forced >| log.txt; cat log.txt
{ echo header; for i in 1 2; do echo "row $i"; done; } > table.txt
cat table.txt
challenge: Write a function run_quiet that runs its arguments as a command with stdout discarded but stderr kept, and prints "ok" or "failed (N)". Test it with ls . and with ls /nonexistent (whose error message you should redirect to /dev/null at the call site so only the status line prints).
question: Where does stderr go in `cmd 2>&1 > out`?
correct: To the original stdout, because 2>&1 is applied before stdout is redirected
wrong: Nowhere; this is a syntax error
reasoning: Redirections are applied left to right; 2>&1 copies the destination of fd 1 at that moment.
expectedStdout:
a.txt: out err 
via pipe: err
b.txt: out
c.txt has 2 lines
first
second
noclobber refused to overwrite
forced
header
row 1
row 2

title: Here-documents and here-strings
body: A here-document feeds lines of the script itself to a command's standard input: cmd <<EOF ... EOF. The terminator must appear alone on its own line, exactly as written.

If the delimiter word is quoted (<<'EOF' or <<"EOF"), the body is completely literal. Unquoted, the body undergoes parameter expansion, command substitution and arithmetic expansion — useful for templates, dangerous when the body contains $ meant literally. Quote the delimiter by default and unquote it only when you want expansion.

<<-EOF strips leading tab characters (not spaces) from body lines and the terminator, which lets you indent here-documents inside functions — but only with real tabs, which many editors convert to spaces.
A here-string, cmd <<< "$text", feeds one string plus a trailing newline to stdin. It is the concise way to give a variable to read, a regex tool or bc without echo and a pipe.

Here-documents are a convenient way to write files from scripts: cat > config.ini <<'EOF'. For generated files containing user data, still prefer printf with explicit quoting so values cannot break the file's format.
code:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
name=ada
cat <<EOF
Hello $name, today has $((24 * 60)) minutes.
EOF
cat <<'EOF'
Literal: $name and $((1 + 1)) stay as typed.
EOF
indented() {
	cat <<-EOF
		tabs removed for $name
	EOF
}
indented
read -r first rest <<< 'one two three'
echo "first=$first rest=$rest"
tr '[:lower:]' '[:upper:]' <<< "here-string for $name"
challenge: Write a function make_config that writes a file app.ini from a here-document containing [server], host=HOST and port=PORT lines, with HOST and PORT taken from its two arguments. Call it with example.org 8443 and print the file.
question: What changes when a here-document delimiter is quoted, as in <<'EOF'?
correct: The body is taken literally, with no expansions
wrong: The body is sent to stderr
reasoning: Quoting any part of the delimiter disables expansion inside the body.
expectedStdout:
Hello ada, today has 1440 minutes.
Literal: $name and $((1 + 1)) stay as typed.
tabs removed for ada
first=one rest=two three
HERE-STRING FOR ADA

title: Managing descriptors with exec
body: exec without a command applies redirections to the current shell itself. exec > log.txt sends all further stdout of the script to log.txt; exec 2>&1 merges stderr into it. This is how scripts start logging everything from one point on.

Additional descriptors keep files open across many commands: exec 3< input.txt opens input for reading on fd 3, and read -r line <&3 (or read -u 3 line) reads the next line from it. Two files can then be read in parallel, line by line.

Bash can allocate a free descriptor for you: exec {fd}> file stores the number (10 or higher) in the variable fd. Use it as >&"$fd" and close it with exec {fd}>&-. This avoids clashes with descriptors used by other code.

Save and restore a stream by duplicating it first: exec {saved}>&1 > file ... exec >&"$saved" {saved}>&-. Closing descriptors you opened matters in long-running scripts: each open descriptor is a resource, and an unclosed write end can keep a reader waiting forever.

exec with a command replaces the shell process with that command — nothing after it runs. Wrapper scripts end with exec real-program "$@" so that signals and exit statuses go directly to the real program.
code:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
printf '%s\n' a b c > left.txt
printf '%s\n' 1 2 3 > right.txt
exec 3< left.txt 4< right.txt
while read -r l <&3 && read -r r <&4; do
    echo "$l$r"
done
exec 3<&- 4<&-
exec {log}> log.txt
echo "allocated fd >= 10: $(( log >= 10 ))"
echo 'to the log' >&"$log"
exec {log}>&-
exec {saved}>&1 > captured.txt
echo 'this line goes to captured.txt'
exec >&"$saved" {saved}>&-
echo "restored; captured: $(cat captured.txt), log: $(cat log.txt)"
challenge: Open notes.txt for writing on an automatically allocated descriptor, write three numbered lines to it in a loop through that descriptor, close it, and print the file.
solution:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
exec {out}> notes.txt
for i in 1 2 3; do
    echo "note $i" >&"$out"
done
exec {out}>&-
cat notes.txt
question: What does `exec {fd}> file` do?
correct: Opens file for writing on a free descriptor number stored in fd
wrong: Writes the descriptor number into file
reasoning: The {varname} form asks Bash to allocate a descriptor of 10 or above and record its number.
expectedStdout:
a1
b2
c3
allocated fd >= 10: 1
restored; captured: this line goes to captured.txt, log: to the log

title: Reading input with read
body: read reads one line from standard input, splits it with IFS and assigns the fields to the named variables, the last variable receiving the remainder. With no name, the whole line goes into REPLY. It returns non-zero at end of file, which is what ends while read loops.

Always use -r. Without it, backslashes in the input are treated as escapes and line continuations, silently changing data. ShellCheck warns about read without -r (SC2162). Combine with IFS= to keep leading and trailing whitespace.

Other options: -p prompt prints a prompt to stderr (interactive input only), -s hides typed characters for passwords, -n N returns after N characters, -N N reads exactly N characters ignoring delimiters, -d c stops at character c instead of newline (-d '' means NUL), -t seconds times out (status above 128), -a name fills an array and -u fd reads from a descriptor.
-e uses Readline for line editing in interactive shells, and Bash 5.3 adds -E, which also enables Bash's own programmable completion while reading. Both only matter when input comes from a terminal.

A final line without a trailing newline makes read return failure even though it filled the variable. Process it with while IFS= read -r line || [[ -n $line ]]. Timeouts with -t 0 test whether input is available without reading anything.
challenge: Read key=value lines from a here-document into an associative array, skipping blank lines and lines starting with #, then print the keys in sorted order with their values. Input: "# config", "name=demo", "", "port=8080".
solution:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
declare -A conf=()
while IFS= read -r line || [[ -n $line ]]; do
    [[ -z $line || $line == \#* ]] && continue
    conf[${line%%=*}]=${line#*=}
done <<'EOF'
# config
name=demo

port=8080
EOF
while IFS= read -r key; do
    echo "$key=${conf[$key]}"
done < <(printf '%s\n' "${!conf[@]}" | sort)
question: Why should read almost always be used with -r?
correct: Without -r, backslashes in the input are interpreted and can alter the data
wrong: -r is required to read from files
reasoning: -r keeps backslashes literal; IFS= is what preserves surrounding whitespace.
expectedStdout:
with -r: path\to\file
without -r: pathtofile
[  spaced  ]
REPLY=into REPLY
first 3: ABC
up to ;: one
timed out (status >128)
processed: last line, no newline

title: NUL-safe file name handling
body: A Unix file name may contain any byte except / and NUL — including spaces, newlines, quotes, glob characters and leading dashes. Line-based processing (ls | while read, for f in $(find ...)) breaks on such names. The only delimiter that cannot occur in a path is the NUL byte.

Produce NUL-separated lists with find -print0, printf '%s\0', or git ls-files -z; consume them with read -r -d '' in a while loop, mapfile -d '', xargs -0 and sort -z. Bash variables cannot contain NUL, so NULs work only as separators between values.

Globs are already safe: for f in *.txt gives each name as one word, however strange. Prefer globs (with nullglob) when you only need names in one directory, and find -print0 when you need recursion or filters.
Leading dashes are the other trap: a file named -rf passed to rm becomes an option. Use -- to end options (rm -- "$f") or prefix relative names with ./ (rm ./*).
find -exec cmd {} + passes many names directly to the command with no parsing at all, and is often the simplest safe choice.
code:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
mkdir -p tricky
touch 'tricky/plain.txt' 'tricky/with space.txt' $'tricky/new\nline.txt' 'tricky/-dash.txt'
printf 'naive line count: %s\n' "$(find tricky -type f | wc -l | tr -d ' ')"
count=0
while IFS= read -r -d '' f; do
    (( ++count ))
done < <(find tricky -type f -print0)
echo "NUL-safe count: $count"
# shellcheck disable=SC2016  # $# belongs to the inner shell
find tricky -type f -exec bash -c 'echo "-exec + passed $# names in one batch"' _ {} +
cd tricky || exit
for f in *; do printf '%q\n' "$f"; done
rm -- -dash.txt && echo 'removed -dash.txt safely'
challenge: Count the total bytes of all .log files under a directory tree that contains a file named "a b.log" (5 bytes) and "c.log" (3 bytes), using find -print0 and a NUL-safe loop with wc -c reading each file via redirection.
solution:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
mkdir -p logs/sub
printf 'hello' > 'logs/a b.log'
printf 'abc' > logs/sub/c.log
total=0
while IFS= read -r -d '' f; do
    bytes=$(wc -c < "$f")
    total=$(( total + bytes ))
done < <(find logs -type f -name '*.log' -print0)
echo "total bytes: $total"
question: Which character can never appear in a Unix path and so is a safe separator?
correct: The NUL byte
reasoning: Paths may contain every byte except NUL (and / separates components), so NUL-delimited lists are unambiguous.
expectedStdout:
naive line count: 5
NUL-safe count: 4
-exec + passed 4 names in one batch
-dash.txt
$'new\nline.txt'
plain.txt
with\ space.txt
removed -dash.txt safely

title: Pipelines, PIPESTATUS and pipefail
body: cmd1 | cmd2 connects cmd1's stdout to cmd2's stdin; all parts start at the same time and run concurrently. |& also sends stderr through the pipe (shorthand for 2>&1 |).

By default a pipeline's exit status is that of its last command, so failing_command | sort succeeds. set -o pipefail makes the status the rightmost non-zero one, so a failure anywhere is reported. The PIPESTATUS array holds every part's status from the most recent pipeline; copy it immediately, since the next command replaces it.

pipefail has a famous false alarm: when a reader exits early (head -n 1, grep -q), the writer may be killed by SIGPIPE and report 141 (128+13). Under pipefail the pipeline then "fails" although nothing went wrong. Handle it by checking PIPESTATUS explicitly, or by avoiding early-exit readers when the writer's status matters.

Each part of a pipeline runs in a subshell, so variables assigned in a while loop at the end of a pipe are lost. shopt -s lastpipe runs the last part in the current shell when job control is off (always true in scripts), keeping those variables.
Prefer one tool over long chains where you can: grep pattern file | wc -l is grep -c pattern file, and cat file | cmd is cmd < file. Fewer processes are faster and have fewer failure points.
code:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
false | true; echo "default status: $?"
false | true; echo "PIPESTATUS: ${PIPESTATUS[*]}"
set -o pipefail
false | true; echo "with pipefail: $?"
yes | head -n 1 > /dev/null; statuses=("${PIPESTATUS[@]}")
echo "yes|head statuses: ${statuses[*]} (141 = SIGPIPE)"
set +o pipefail
total=0
printf '%s\n' 1 2 3 | while read -r n; do total=$((total + n)); done
echo "without lastpipe: $total"
shopt -s lastpipe
printf '%s\n' 1 2 3 | while read -r n; do total=$((total + n)); done
echo "with lastpipe: $total"
challenge: Write a function safe_first that prints the first line of a command's output (given as arguments) and returns the command's own status, ignoring SIGPIPE caused by head. Test with printf '%s\n' a b and with false.
question: Why can `yes | head -n 1` fail under pipefail?
correct: yes is killed by SIGPIPE when head exits, giving status 141
reasoning: An early-exiting reader makes the writer die with SIGPIPE (128+13), which pipefail reports as failure.
expectedStdout:
default status: 0
PIPESTATUS: 1 0
with pipefail: 1
yes|head statuses: 141 0 (141 = SIGPIPE)
without lastpipe: 0
with lastpipe: 6

title: Subshells versus the current shell
body: A subshell is a forked copy of the shell. It inherits all variables (exported or not), functions, options and open descriptors, but changes it makes — variables, cd, umask, traps, shell options — disappear when it exits. Parentheses ( ... ), $( ... ), each pipeline part (except the last with lastpipe), & background commands and <( ) all create subshells.

{ ...; } braces group commands in the current shell, so their changes persist. Choose parentheses when you want isolation — a temporary cd, a changed IFS or shell option — and braces when you want the effects.
$BASH_SUBSHELL counts nesting depth and $BASHPID gives the real process ID, while $$ always reports the main shell. These help when debugging where code actually runs.
exit inside a subshell only leaves the subshell. That is why `cmd || ( echo error; exit 1 )` does not stop the script; use braces: cmd || { echo error >&2; exit 1; }.
Forking costs time: thousands of $(...) in a loop are measurably slow. The next lesson shows how to avoid forks for capturing output.
challenge: Write a function in_dir that runs a command (its remaining arguments) inside the directory given as its first argument without changing the caller's directory, using a subshell body. Use it to print the base name of $PWD inside /tmp's parent (/) and show the caller's directory is unchanged.
solution:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
in_dir() (
    cd "$1" || exit
    shift
    "$@"
)
in_dir / pwd
echo "caller still in: ${PWD##*/}"
question: Why does `cmd || ( echo failed; exit 1 )` not stop the script?
correct: exit only ends the subshell created by the parentheses
reasoning: Use { echo failed; exit 1; } so exit runs in the current shell.
expectedStdout:
subshell: x=inner pwd=/ depth=1
after ( ): x=outer pwd=work
after { }: x=braced
depth inside $(): 1
exit in ( ) only leaves the subshell
still running
exit in { } leaves the shell
fail_hard status: 1

title: Command substitution, including ${ cmd; } (Bash 5.3)
body: $(command) runs command in a subshell and replaces itself with the command's standard output, minus all trailing newlines. Quote it ("$(cmd)") to avoid word splitting and globbing. It nests cleanly: "$(dirname "$(pwd)")". The old backquote form `cmd` needs escaping to nest and should not be used in new code.
Because the trailing newlines are stripped, $(printf 'a\n\n') is just a. To keep them, append a sentinel character and remove it afterwards: out=$(cmd; printf x); out=${out%x}.

Bash 5.3 adds ${ command; }: the command runs in the current shell, without forking, and its output is captured the same way. Variable assignments and cd inside it persist, and it is much faster in loops. The space (or newline) after ${ and the final ; or newline before } are required.

${| command; } is a variant that captures nothing from stdout; instead its value is whatever the command assigns to REPLY. REPLY is local to the substitution, so the caller's REPLY is untouched. This lets functions return values with no subshell and no output parsing.

These forms are unknown to older shells — macOS /bin/bash 3.2 reports "bad substitution" — so use them only in scripts that require Bash 5.3. Within such scripts they are the preferred way to capture output from shell functions.
challenge: Write a function next_id that increments a global counter and assigns "id-N" to REPLY. Generate three ids with ${| next_id; } into an array and print them, then print the counter (3) to show no subshell lost the increments.
solution:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
counter=0
next_id() {
    counter=$((counter + 1))
    REPLY="id-$counter"
}
ids=()
for _ in 1 2 3; do
    ids+=("${| next_id; }")
done
echo "${ids[*]}"
echo "counter=$counter"
question: What is the key difference between $(cmd) and ${ cmd; }?
correct: ${ cmd; } runs in the current shell, so no fork happens and side effects persist
reasoning: Both capture stdout and strip trailing newlines; the 5.3 form avoids the subshell.
expectedStdout:
classic: work
stripped: [a]
kept 3 chars
same process: 1, count=1
shout=QUIET REPLY=untouched

title: Process substitution
body: <(command) runs command asynchronously and expands to a file name — such as /dev/fd/63 — from which its output can be read. >(command) gives a file name to write to, whose data becomes the command's input. They let programs that only accept file names work with command output.

Classic uses: diff <(sort a) <(sort b) compares sorted versions without temporary files; while read ... done < <(cmd) feeds a loop without a pipeline subshell; tee >(gzip > log.gz) >(wc -l > count) sends one stream to several consumers.

Process substitutions run in the background. Their exit status is not available as $? of the main command; since Bash 5.1 (and improved in 5.3), $! holds the PID of the last one, and wait "$!" collects its status.

Output written to >(...) may still be in flight when the main command returns, so a later command reading the result can race. Wait for it ($! and wait) or use a regular pipeline when ordering matters.
Process substitution is a Bash/ksh/zsh feature; it needs /dev/fd or named pipes and is not POSIX sh.
code:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
printf '%s\n' pear apple fig > a.txt
printf '%s\n' fig pear apple kiwi > b.txt
diff <(sort a.txt) <(sort b.txt) && echo same || echo 'diff shows kiwi only in b'
echo "the substitution is a file name: $(echo <(true) | sed 's/[0-9]*$/N/')"
printf '%s\n' one two three | tee >(wc -l | tr -d ' ' > count.txt) > copy.txt
wait "$!"
echo "copied $(wc -l < copy.txt | tr -d ' ') lines, counted $(cat count.txt)"
max=0
while read -r n; do (( n > max )) && max=$n; done < <(printf '%s\n' 4 11 7)
echo "max kept after loop: $max"
challenge: Use comm with two process substitutions to print the words present in both lists "red green blue" and "blue yellow red" (one per line, sorted).
solution:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
comm -12 <(printf '%s\n' red green blue | sort) <(printf '%s\n' blue yellow red | sort)
question: What does <(cmd) expand to?
correct: A file name, such as /dev/fd/63, connected to cmd's output
reasoning: Process substitution turns a command's output into a readable path for programs expecting files.
expectedStdout:
2a3
> kiwi
diff shows kiwi only in b
the substitution is a file name: /dev/fd/N
copied 3 lines, counted 3
max kept after loop: 11

title: Background jobs, wait and wait -n
body: cmd & starts cmd in the background and continues immediately; $! holds its PID. wait with no arguments waits for all background children; wait PID waits for one and returns its exit status. A script that starts jobs should always wait for them, otherwise their failures go unnoticed and they may outlive the script.

wait -n waits for the next job to finish, whichever it is, and returns its status. With -p var (Bash 5.1+) it also stores the finished job's PID in var, so you can tell which task ended. This is the building block of a concurrency limiter: start jobs until N are running, then wait -n before starting the next.
Background jobs share the terminal's stdout and stderr, so their output interleaves unpredictably. Give each job its own output file, or collect and print results after waiting, when order matters.
Job control (fg, bg, %1, Ctrl-Z) is an interactive feature and is off in scripts. In scripts, think in terms of PIDs and wait.

Since Bash 5.3, wait -n can also report process substitutions and already-notified jobs, behaving more like plain wait. Write loops that track their own PIDs instead of assuming which job will finish first.
code:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
task() { sleep "$1"; echo "task $2 done" > "out.$2"; return "$3"; }
task 1 a 0 &
pid_a=$!
task 0.1 b 4 &
wait -n -p finished
echo "first to finish exited $? (it was $([[ $finished == "$pid_a" ]] && echo a || echo b))"
wait "$pid_a"; echo "a exited $?"
cat out.a out.b
max_jobs=2 running=0 results=()
for n in 1 2 3 4 5; do
    if (( running >= max_jobs )); then wait -n; (( running-- )); fi
    { sleep 0.05; echo $(( n * n )) > "sq.$n"; } &
    (( ++running ))
done
wait
for n in 1 2 3 4 5; do results+=("$(< "sq.$n")"); done
echo "squares: ${results[*]}"
challenge: Run three background tasks that exit with statuses 0, 3 and 0, wait for each by PID, and print how many failed (1).
solution:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
pids=()
for status in 0 3 0; do
    ( sleep 0.05; exit "$status" ) &
    pids+=("$!")
done
failed=0
for pid in "${pids[@]}"; do
    wait "$pid" || (( ++failed ))
done
echo "failed: $failed"
question: What does `wait -n -p var` do?
correct: Waits for the next background job to finish and stores its PID in var
wrong: Waits for all jobs and stores their count in var
Starts var as a new job
reasoning: -n waits for any single job; -p records which PID finished, enabling concurrency-limited loops.
expectedStdout:
first to finish exited 4 (it was b)
a exited 0
task a done
task b done
squares: 1 4 9 16 25

title: Coprocesses
body: coproc NAME { commands; } starts commands in the background with two-way pipes: NAME[0] is a descriptor for reading its output and NAME[1] for writing to its input, and NAME_PID holds its PID. It is how a script keeps a long-running helper (bc, a database client, a line-oriented server) open and talks to it repeatedly.

Write a request with printf ... >&"${NAME[1]}" and read the answer with read -r reply <&"${NAME[0]}". Make sure the helper does not buffer its output: many programs buffer when writing to a pipe, which deadlocks a request/response conversation. Line-oriented tools often have an option to flush, or use stdbuf where available.

When finished, close the write end — copy it to a plain variable and close that, in=${NAME[1]}; exec {in}>&- — so the helper sees end of input and exits, then wait "$NAME_PID". Name every coprocess; unnamed ones are called COPROC.
Since Bash 5.3 multiple coprocesses can be active at once by default (MULTIPLE_COPROCS). Each needs a distinct name.

Coprocesses are powerful but easy to deadlock. For one-shot work, a pipeline or process substitution is simpler; reach for coproc when the per-request cost of starting a process would otherwise dominate.
code:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
coproc CALC { while read -r a b; do echo $(( a * b )); done; }
for pair in '6 7' '12 12' '3 1000'; do
    printf '%s\n' "$pair" >&"${CALC[1]}"
    read -r answer <&"${CALC[0]}"
    echo "$pair -> $answer"
done
in=${CALC[1]}
exec {in}>&-
wait "$CALC_PID"
echo "helper exited with $?"
challenge: Start a coprocess named UPPER that converts each input line to uppercase with a read loop (no external tools), send it the words alpha and beta, print each reply, then close it and wait for it.
question: Why can a request/response coprocess deadlock with an external program?
correct: The program may buffer its output when writing to a pipe, so the reply never arrives
wrong: Bash closes the pipe after one line
reasoning: Block-buffered output waits for a full buffer; the script waits for a reply; neither progresses.

title: set -e, set -u and their real limits
body: set -e (errexit) exits the script when a command fails. set -u (nounset) treats expansion of an unset variable as an error. set -o pipefail makes pipelines report failures anywhere. Together, set -euo pipefail is often called "strict mode" and catches many mistakes early.

errexit is deliberately ignored in many contexts: the condition of if, while and until; any command in a && or || list except the last; commands negated with !; and — the big surprise — everything inside a function that is itself called from one of those contexts. `if myfunc; then` disables errexit for the whole body of myfunc.

Command substitution does not inherit errexit by default, and local x=$(cmd) hides the failure anyway. shopt -s inherit_errexit makes $(...) inherit set -e. Arithmetic (( expr )) returning 1 for a zero result also triggers errexit, a common source of mysterious exits with (( count++ )).

set -u fails on ${unset}, but ${var-default}, ${var:-default} and [[ -v var ]] are safe ways to test optional variables. "$@" with no arguments is fine with set -u since Bash 4.4; ${array[@]} of an empty array is too.

Strict mode is a safety net, not error handling. Check the commands whose failure you can anticipate explicitly (if ! cmd; then ...), give a useful message, and let errexit catch the rest. Some teams avoid set -e entirely for this reason; whichever you choose, know these rules.
code:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail
shopt -s inherit_errexit
step() { false; echo '  step continued after false'; }
if step; then echo '  if step: errexit was off inside the function'; fi
false || echo '  failure on the left of || is allowed'
count=0
(( count++ )) || true
echo "  count=$count (|| true kept (( )) from exiting)"
echo "  optional: ${MAYBE_UNSET:-default}"
[[ -v MAYBE_UNSET ]] || echo '  -v test is safe under set -u'
# shellcheck disable=SC2154  # deliberately unset to trigger nounset
( echo "  ${missing_var}" ) 2>/dev/null || echo "  set -u stopped the subshell with status $?"
step
echo 'never printed: plain step call exits the script'
challenge: Write a script under set -euo pipefail with a function require_file that prints "error: missing NAME" to stderr and returns 1 when a file is absent. Call it for an existing file (print "ok") and then, explicitly handled with if !, for a missing one, printing "handled missing input" and exiting with status 3.
solution:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail
require_file() {
    if [[ ! -f $1 ]]; then
        echo "error: missing $1" >&2
        return 1
    fi
}
touch present.txt
require_file present.txt && echo ok
if ! require_file absent.txt 2>/dev/null; then
    echo 'handled missing input'
    exit 3
fi
question: Why does `if myfunc; then` disable set -e inside myfunc?
correct: errexit is ignored for every command executed as part of an if condition, including function bodies
wrong: if runs the function in a subshell
set -e only applies to external programs
reasoning: Bash suppresses errexit throughout a condition context, so failures inside the function do not exit.

title: trap: cleanup and signals
body: trap 'commands' SIGNAL... registers commands to run when the shell receives a signal or reaches a pseudo-signal. EXIT runs when the shell exits for any reason — normal end, exit, errexit or a fatal signal it handles — and is the right place for cleanup such as deleting temporary files.

INT (Ctrl-C) and TERM (the default of kill) are the signals scripts most often handle. A handler should clean up and then exit with the conventional status 128+N, or re-raise the signal (trap - INT; kill -INT $$) so the caller sees that the script was interrupted.

Use single quotes so the trap command is expanded when the trap runs, not when it is set: trap 'rm -f -- "$tmp"' EXIT uses the value of tmp at exit time. Calling a function from the trap keeps complex handlers readable.

trap -p lists traps as re-usable commands; Bash 5.3 adds trap -P to print only the action for each signal named. Also new in 5.3, BASH_TRAPSIG holds the number of the signal whose trap is running, so one handler can serve several signals.

Traps are reset in subshells (except that the EXIT trap of a subshell is its own), ignored signals stay ignored, and SIGKILL and SIGSTOP cannot be trapped at all. A script cannot guarantee cleanup after kill -9; design so that leftover files are harmless.
code:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# shellcheck disable=SC2329  # both functions are invoked by traps
cleanup() { echo "cleanup: removing the work directory (status was $1)"; rm -rf -- "$work"; }
work=$(mktemp -d)
trap 'cleanup $?' EXIT
on_signal() { echo "handler: signal $BASH_TRAPSIG"; }
trap on_signal TERM INT
trap -P TERM
kill -TERM $$
kill -INT $$
touch "$work/data"
echo "work dir has: $(ls "$work")"
exit 7
challenge: Write a script that creates a temporary file, installs an EXIT trap that deletes it and prints "deleted", handles TERM by printing "terminating" and exiting 143, then sends itself TERM. Show the trap order: terminating, then deleted.
solution:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
tmp=$(mktemp)
trap 'rm -f -- "$tmp"; echo deleted' EXIT
trap 'echo terminating; exit 143' TERM
kill -TERM $$
echo 'not reached'
question: Which trap runs on normal completion, explicit exit and errexit alike?
correct: EXIT
reasoning: The EXIT pseudo-signal fires whenever the shell exits, making it the place for cleanup.
expectedStdout:
on_signal
handler: signal 15
handler: signal 2
work dir has: data
cleanup: removing the work directory (status was 7)

title: Temporary files and directories
body: Never create temporary files with predictable names like /tmp/myscript.$$: another user can pre-create or symlink that path, and two copies of the script collide. mktemp creates a uniquely named file with permissions 600 and prints its path; mktemp -d creates a private directory.

Pair every mktemp with an EXIT trap that removes it, set immediately after creation. If you create several temporary paths, make one temporary directory and put everything in it, so one rm -rf cleans up.

mktemp honours TMPDIR, so users and CI systems can redirect temporary storage. Pass a template when you want a recognizable name: mktemp "${TMPDIR:-/tmp}/backup.XXXXXX" — the Xs are replaced by random characters. GNU and BSD mktemp differ in some options, so stick to plain mktemp, -d and a template ending in XXXXXX for portability.
umask controls the permissions of new files. umask 077 at the top of a script that handles secrets makes every file it creates private.
Guard destructive commands: rm -rf -- "${work:?}" fails safely if work is unexpectedly empty instead of operating on the wrong path, and the -- protects against names starting with a dash.
code:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail
work=$(mktemp -d)
trap 'rm -rf -- "${work:?}"' EXIT
file=$(mktemp "$work/report.XXXXXX")
echo "name pattern ok: $([[ ${file##*/} =~ ^report\.[A-Za-z0-9]{6}$ ]] && echo yes)"
# shellcheck disable=SC2012  # ls -l is used only for its permission column
perm=$(ls -l "$file" | cut -c1-10)
echo "mktemp file permissions: $perm"
# shellcheck disable=SC2012
( umask 077; touch "$work/secret"; ls -l "$work/secret" | cut -c1-10 )
unset work_typo
if ! message=$( ( rm -rf -- "${work_typo:?refusing to delete an empty path}" ) 2>&1 ); then
    echo "guarded: ${message##*: }"
fi
challenge: Write a function with_temp_dir that creates a temporary directory, runs the given command inside it in a subshell, and always removes the directory afterwards (even if the command fails), returning the command's status. Run it with touch x and with false, printing each status and whether the directory still exists.
solution:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
with_temp_dir() {
    local dir status
    dir=$(mktemp -d)
    ( cd "$dir" && "$@" )
    status=$?
    rm -rf -- "$dir"
    [[ -d $dir ]] && echo 'leaked' || echo 'cleaned up'
    return "$status"
}
with_temp_dir touch x; echo "status $?"
with_temp_dir false; echo "status $?"
question: Why is /tmp/script.$$ a poor temporary file name?
correct: It is predictable, so another process can pre-create or symlink it
reasoning: mktemp creates an unpredictable name atomically with safe permissions.

title: ERR traps, stack traces and die
body: trap 'handler' ERR runs whenever a command fails under the same rules that errexit uses (so not in if conditions or && lists). Inside the handler, $? is the failing status, BASH_COMMAND the command text and LINENO or BASH_LINENO the line.

By default the ERR trap is not inherited by functions, command substitutions or subshells. set -o errtrace (set -E) makes it inherited, which you almost always want together with an ERR trap. set -o functrace (set -T) does the same for DEBUG and RETURN traps.
The caller builtin and the arrays FUNCNAME, BASH_SOURCE and BASH_LINENO describe the call stack. Walking them in the handler produces a stack trace: each frame's function, file and line.

A die function — print a message to stderr and exit non-zero — makes intentional failure explicit: [[ -r $config ]] || die "cannot read $config". Use exit codes consistently: 1 general failure, 2 usage error, and documented specific codes for distinct conditions.
Report errors where the user can act on them: say what failed, with which input, and what to do next. Messages like "error" alone waste the reader's time.
challenge: Write a die function that prints "fatal: MESSAGE" to stderr and exits with an optional status (default 1). Use it to reject a missing argument: call a main function with no arguments, which should print "usage: main NAME" via die with status 2. Print nothing to stdout.
question: Why combine an ERR trap with set -E (errtrace)?
correct: Without it, the ERR trap does not fire for failures inside functions and subshells
wrong: set -E makes the trap run twice
ERR traps require it to be parsed
set -E disables errexit inside the trap
reasoning: ERR traps are not inherited by functions, command substitutions and subshells unless errtrace is enabled.
expectedStdout: starting

title: Idempotent, atomic and locked operations
body: An idempotent script can run twice and end in the same state: mkdir -p instead of mkdir, ln -sfn instead of ln -s, checks like [[ -e $target ]] || create. Idempotency makes reruns after a partial failure safe — the most common way scripts are recovered.

Writing a file in place risks leaving it half-written if the script is interrupted. Write to a temporary file in the same directory and mv it over the target: rename within one filesystem is atomic, so readers see either the old or the new file, never a mix.

Prevent two copies of a script from running at once with a lock. mkdir is atomic and portable: if mkdir "$lockdir" 2>/dev/null; then ... else exit; fi, with an EXIT trap that removes the directory. On Linux, flock on a file descriptor is an alternative, but it is not installed on macOS by default.

Guard paths used in destructive commands: ${dir:?} on empty values, -- before arguments, and never rm -rf "$dir/"* with an unchecked variable. A dry-run mode that prints actions instead of performing them (via a run function that echoes or executes) makes risky scripts reviewable.
Return clear statuses and print what changed. "created X", "X already present" output tells the operator exactly what the rerun did.
code:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail
ensure_dir() {
    if [[ -d $1 ]]; then echo "exists: $1"; else mkdir -p -- "$1"; echo "created: $1"; fi
}
ensure_dir out; ensure_dir out
write_atomic() {
    local target=$1 tmp
    tmp=$(mktemp "${target%/*}/.${target##*/}.XXXXXX")
    cat > "$tmp"
    mv -f -- "$tmp" "$target"
}
printf 'version=1\n' | write_atomic out/config
printf 'version=2\n' | write_atomic out/config
echo "config: $(cat out/config); leftovers: $(find out -name '.config.*' | wc -l | tr -d ' ')"
lock=out/.lock
if mkdir "$lock" 2>/dev/null; then
    trap 'rmdir "$lock"' EXIT
    echo 'lock acquired'
    mkdir "$lock" 2>/dev/null || echo 'second instance would be refused'
fi
DRY_RUN=1
run() { if (( DRY_RUN )); then printf 'would run:'; printf ' %q' "$@"; echo; else "$@"; fi; }
run rm -rf -- 'out/old data'
challenge: Write a function append_once that adds a line to a file only if that exact line is not already present (use grep -Fxq), printing "added" or "present". Call it three times with the lines "PATH=/opt/bin", "PATH=/opt/bin", "EDITOR=vi" on profile.txt and print the file.
solution:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
append_once() {
    local line=$1 file=$2
    if [[ -f $file ]] && grep -Fxq -- "$line" "$file"; then
        echo present
    else
        printf '%s\n' "$line" >> "$file"
        echo added
    fi
}
append_once 'PATH=/opt/bin' profile.txt
append_once 'PATH=/opt/bin' profile.txt
append_once 'EDITOR=vi' profile.txt
cat profile.txt

title: eval, printf -v and generating shell code safely
body: eval concatenates its arguments and parses the result as shell code a second time. Anything inside a value — ;, $(...), quotes — becomes code. eval "echo $input" with input='x; rm -rf ~' runs the rm. Most uses of eval are attempts to do something Bash already supports safely.

Safer replacements: indirect expansion ${!name} or namerefs for dynamic variable names; printf -v "$name" '%s' "$value" to assign to a computed name; arrays for dynamic commands; declare -A for computed keys.

printf -v var fmt args formats directly into a variable, with no subshell and no word-splitting surprises — also the fastest way to build strings in loops. Validate the variable name first, because a name like a[$(cmd)] is itself code.

When code generation is truly needed — writing a script, an ssh remote command, a config read back by a shell — quote every value with printf %q or ${var@Q}. The result re-parses to exactly the original value.
declare -p var produces a re-loadable definition of a variable, including arrays and attributes; sourcing that output recreates it. This is a clean way to save shell state to a file.
code:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
input='x; echo INJECTED'
eval "echo $input"
echo ---
printf -v greeting '%s, %s!' Hello 'world; echo nope'
echo "$greeting"
name=color
[[ $name =~ ^[A-Za-z_][A-Za-z0-9_]*$ ]] && printf -v "$name" '%s' blue
echo "color=${!name}"
remote="ls -- $(printf '%q' 'my dir; rm x')"
echo "safe remote command: $remote"
declare -A saved=([a]=1 [b]='two words')
declare -p saved > state.sh
unset saved
# shellcheck source=/dev/null
source state.sh
echo "restored: ${saved[b]}"

correct: Validate the name, then use printf -v "$name" '%s' "$value"
reasoning: printf -v assigns without re-parsing the value; validating the name prevents subscript code execution.

title: Debugging: xtrace, PS4, BASH_XTRACEFD and DEBUG traps
body: set -x (xtrace) prints each command after expansion, prefixed by PS4, before running it — the fastest way to see what a script really does, including how quoting and expansions turned out. set +x turns it off; bash -x script.sh traces a whole run.

Customize PS4 to show where each line came from: PS4='+ ${BASH_SOURCE[0]##*/}:${LINENO}:${FUNCNAME[0]:-main}: '. Use single quotes so the variables expand each time a trace line is printed. The first character of PS4 is repeated to show nesting depth.

Trace output goes to stderr by default, mixing with real errors. BASH_XTRACEFD=N sends it to descriptor N instead: exec {trace}> trace.log; BASH_XTRACEFD=$trace. Then the trace can be inspected without disturbing normal output.

bash -n script checks syntax without running anything — useful in CI. trap '...' DEBUG runs before every simple command, with BASH_COMMAND holding the command about to run; it can implement step tracing or timing. caller prints the line and function of the current call site.
Debug systematically: reproduce with the smallest input, trace only the suspect section, print values with declare -p or printf '[%s]\n' to see boundaries, and run ShellCheck before guessing.
code:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
exec {trace}> trace.log
BASH_XTRACEFD=$trace
PS4='+ ${FUNCNAME[0]:-main}:${LINENO}: '
greet() { local who=${1^}; echo "hello $who"; }
set -x
greet 'ada lovelace'
set +x
exec {trace}>&-
echo '--- trace.log ---'
cat trace.log
where() { caller 0 | cut -d' ' -f1-2; }
where
steps=0
trap '(( ++steps ))' DEBUG
true; true; true
trap - DEBUG
echo "DEBUG trap saw $steps commands"
challenge: Enable xtrace only around a loop that doubles the numbers 1 2 3, sending the trace to a file via BASH_XTRACEFD with PS4 set to "+ line ${LINENO}: ", then print how many trace lines mention doubled= (3).
solution:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
exec {fd}> loop.trace
BASH_XTRACEFD=$fd
PS4='+ line ${LINENO}: '
set -x
for n in 1 2 3; do
    doubled=$((n * 2))
done
set +x
exec {fd}>&-
echo "doubled=$doubled"
grep -c 'doubled=' loop.trace

correct: The file descriptor that set -x trace output is written to
reasoning: By default trace output goes to stderr; BASH_XTRACEFD redirects it to another descriptor.

stage: 11 · Mastery: debugging, performance, portability and security
title: Performance: builtins first, fewer forks
body: The main cost in shell scripts is starting processes. Each external command and each $(...) subshell is a fork (and usually an exec), costing on the order of a millisecond. A loop that calls sed, cut or $(...) per line over 100,000 lines spends minutes where builtins would take a second.

Prefer built-in features: parameter expansion instead of basename, dirname, cut and sed for single values; [[ =~ ]] instead of grep for one string; $(( )) instead of expr; printf -v or Bash 5.3's ${ ...; } instead of $(...) for capturing; read and mapfile instead of piping through head and tail.

For whole-file processing, the opposite holds: one awk, sed, sort or grep invocation over the file is far faster than a Bash read loop over every line. Move work into a single external process, not one process per line.

Measure rather than guess: time cmd reports elapsed and CPU time. EPOCHREALTIME gives microsecond wall-clock time, and Bash 5.3's BASH_MONOSECONDS reads the monotonic clock, which is immune to clock adjustments. Compare alternatives on realistic input sizes.
Optimize only hot paths. Clear code that runs once is better than clever code that saves a millisecond; a loop over a large dataset is where these techniques matter.
code:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
now_us() { local t=${EPOCHREALTIME/./}; echo "$t"; }
n=300
path=/srv/app/releases/v1.2.3/bin/server
start=$(now_us)
for (( i = 0; i < n; i++ )); do name=$(basename "$path"); done
forked=$(( $(now_us) - start ))
start=$(now_us)
for (( i = 0; i < n; i++ )); do name=${path##*/}; done
builtin=$(( $(now_us) - start ))
echo "same result: $name"
(( forked > builtin * 10 )) && echo "parameter expansion was over 10x faster than basename for $n iterations"
seq 1 50000 > nums.txt
sum=$(awk '{ s += $1 } END { print s }' nums.txt)
echo "one awk process summed 50000 lines: $sum"
challenge: Count how many of the words in a 2000-word array start with "a" two ways — with a loop using [[ ]] and with one printf | grep -c — and print both counts (they must agree). Build the array by repeating the words apple banana avocado cherry 500 times.
solution:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
words=()
for (( i = 0; i < 500; i++ )); do words+=(apple banana avocado cherry); done
count=0
for w in "${words[@]}"; do [[ $w == a* ]] && (( ++count )); done
echo "loop: $count"
echo "grep: $(printf '%s\n' "${words[@]}" | grep -c '^a')"
question: Why is ${path##*/} much faster than $(basename "$path") inside a loop?
correct: It runs inside the shell without starting a process
reasoning: Every $(basename ...) forks and executes a program; parameter expansion costs no process.

title: Portability: POSIX sh, Bash versions and macOS
body: #!/bin/sh promises POSIX shell code. On Debian and Ubuntu /bin/sh is dash; on macOS it is Bash 3.2 in POSIX mode; on Alpine it is BusyBox ash. [[ ]], arrays, local (technically), ${var//a/b}, <( ), $'...', {1..5}, == in [ ] and function name { } are not POSIX. If you need these, use #!/usr/bin/env bash.

Bash itself differs by version. macOS ships 3.2 (2007) as /bin/bash for licensing reasons: no associative arrays, mapfile, ${var,,}, nameref, ;;& or |&. Check BASH_VERSINFO at the top when you rely on newer features and fail with a clear message rather than a confusing syntax error.

External tools differ too: GNU versus BSD sed -i, date, stat, readlink -f, grep -P, find options. Stick to POSIX options, detect the variant (sed --version succeeds only on GNU), or require GNU tools explicitly.

bash --posix or set -o posix makes Bash follow POSIX where they differ — useful for testing that a #!/bin/sh script really is portable, together with running it under dash. ShellCheck checks against the dialect named in the shebang or with -s sh.
Choose deliberately: for scripts run on machines you control, require Bash 5.x and use its features freely; for installers that must run anywhere, write POSIX sh and keep them small.
code:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
require_bash() {
    local major=$1 minor=$2
    if (( BASH_VERSINFO[0] > major || (BASH_VERSINFO[0] == major && BASH_VERSINFO[1] >= minor) )); then
        echo "Bash ${BASH_VERSINFO[0]}.${BASH_VERSINFO[1]} satisfies >= $major.$minor"
    else
        echo "need Bash >= $major.$minor" >&2; return 1
    fi
}
require_bash 4 4
require_bash 99 0 2>&1 || true
cat > portable.sh <<'EOF'
set -- "two words" three
for arg do
    case $arg in
        *" "*) printf '%s has a space\n' "$arg" ;;
        *) printf '%s\n' "$arg" ;;
    esac
done
EOF
sh portable.sh
shellcheck -s sh portable.sh && echo 'ShellCheck: valid POSIX sh'
printf 'a=(1 2)\n[[ -n x ]]\n' > bashism.sh
shellcheck -s sh -f gcc bashism.sh | grep -o 'SC[0-9]*' | sort -u | tr '\n' ' '; echo

case $x in
    *.txt) echo text ;;
esac
EOF

correct: /bin/bash on macOS is Bash 3.2, which has no associative arrays
wrong: zsh is used for every script
reasoning: Use #!/usr/bin/env bash with a modern Bash installed, and check BASH_VERSINFO for required features.

stage: 11 · Mastery: debugging, performance, portability and security
title: Static analysis with ShellCheck
body: ShellCheck reads scripts and reports likely bugs: unquoted expansions (SC2086), read without -r (SC2162), cd without error handling (SC2164), unused or unassigned variables (SC2034, SC2154), useless cat and many portability problems. Each warning has a wiki page explaining the reasoning, at shellcheck.net/wiki/SCxxxx.

It infers the dialect from the shebang; override with -s bash or -s sh. -x follows source statements, and a `# shellcheck source=path` directive tells it where a dynamically computed source path points.

When a warning is a deliberate choice, disable it narrowly: a `# shellcheck disable=SC2086` directive applies to the next command (or to the whole file when placed before the first command), and should carry a comment saying why. Never disable a check just to make output quiet.

A .shellcheckrc file in the project sets defaults such as enabled optional checks (enable=require-variable-braces) or external-sources=true. -S warning raises the minimum severity reported; -f gcc or -f json produce machine-readable output for editors and CI.
Make ShellCheck a gate in CI: every .sh file must pass. Every script in this guide does, except where a lesson deliberately shows a pitfall and declares the expected finding.
code:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
cat > sample.sh <<'EOF'
#!/usr/bin/env bash
files=$(ls *.txt)
for f in $files; do
    cat $f | wc -l
done
read name
cd /tmp
EOF
echo 'findings:'
shellcheck -f gcc sample.sh | grep -o 'SC[0-9]*' | sort | uniq -c | awk '{ print "  " $2 " x" $1 }'
cat > fixed.sh <<'EOF'
#!/usr/bin/env bash
shopt -s nullglob
for f in *.txt; do
    wc -l < "$f"
done
read -r name
echo "$name"
cd /tmp || exit
EOF
shellcheck fixed.sh && echo 'fixed.sh: no findings'
challenge: Write a script file greet.sh containing `echo Hello $1` and run shellcheck on it to print the finding code; then write the fixed version and show that ShellCheck reports nothing.
solution:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# shellcheck disable=SC2016  # the generated scripts must keep $1 literal
printf '#!/usr/bin/env bash\necho Hello $1\n' > greet.sh
shellcheck -f gcc greet.sh | grep -o 'SC[0-9]*'
printf '#!/usr/bin/env bash\necho "Hello $1"\n' > greet.sh
shellcheck greet.sh && echo 'clean'

correct: A narrow disable directive with a comment explaining why
wrong: Rename the variable until it stops warning
Run ShellCheck only on new files
reasoning: Narrow, explained directives keep the remaining checks useful and document intent.

title: Security: injection, PATH, privileges and secrets
body: Treat every external value — arguments, environment, file contents, file names, network data — as data, never as code. The main injection points are eval, sh -c/bash -c strings, ssh remote commands, arithmetic contexts and array subscripts, and unquoted expansions that glob.

To run a command string with user data, pass the data as arguments, not inside the string: bash -c 'grep -- "$1" "$2"' _ "$pattern" "$file". The _ fills $0; the values arrive as positional parameters and are never parsed as code.

Control the environment of privileged scripts: set PATH explicitly (PATH=/usr/bin:/bin), use absolute paths for critical tools, reset IFS, and do not trust inherited variables such as BASH_ENV, LD_PRELOAD or ENV. Bash ignores imported functions with unusual names and has been hardened since Shellshock (2014), but never source files writable by others.

Keep secrets out of command lines (visible in ps) and out of xtrace output. Read them from files with restrictive permissions or from stdin, pass them via environment variables or descriptors, and set +x around code that handles them. umask 077 protects files you create.

Validate early with allow-lists — explicit patterns like ^[a-z0-9-]+$ — rather than trying to block dangerous characters. Run with least privilege, and prefer failing closed: refuse input you do not understand.

title: Project: a tested command-line task manager
body: This project combines the earlier stages into one small but complete tool: todo.sh keeps a task list in a text file and supports add, list and complete subcommands, a -f FILE option, a TODO_FILE environment default and both -h and --help. Read the whole script before running it; every technique in it has its own earlier lesson.

Structure: strict mode at the top; usage and die helpers; one function per subcommand; a main function that parses options with getopts, then dispatches with case; and a final main "$@". Usage errors exit with status 2 and runtime errors with status 1, with every message on stderr.

Data safety: task text is written with printf '%s' so stars, dollar signs and backslashes are stored literally. Completing a task reads the file with mapfile, edits one array element and replaces the file via a mktemp file in the same directory followed by mv, so an interruption never leaves a half-written list. The temporary file starts as a cp -p copy, so the list keeps its permissions (a symlinked list is still replaced by a regular file — a documented limit). Task numbers are limited to nine digits, because longer values would wrap in 64-bit arithmetic and mark the wrong task.

Testing: tests/test_todo.sh runs the tool as a separate process in a fresh temporary directory, compares exact output and exit statuses with a tiny check helper from tests/lib.sh, and removes its directory in an EXIT trap. Tests cover the happy path, invalid numbers, a second completion, missing option arguments, unknown commands, the -f option, the environment default and leftover temporary files.

Exercise levels — Beginner: run the tests, then predict the output of list after adding three tasks and completing the second. Intermediate: add an undo N subcommand that reopens a finished task and refuses an open one. Advanced: add a count subcommand printing "OPEN open of TOTAL", working even when the file does not exist, with tests for each behaviour. The worked answer implements both and adds four checks.

Validation in this guide also runs a mutation check: the completion line is deliberately broken and the suite must fail. A test suite that still passes after a real bug is introduced is not testing that behaviour.
expectedStdout: 2. ship
challenge: Beginner: run bash tests/test_todo.sh and read every check. Intermediate: add undo N. Advanced: add count with tests (open and total, including a missing file).
question: Why does complete write to a mktemp file in the same directory and then mv it?
correct: A same-filesystem rename replaces the list atomically, so an interruption cannot leave a partial file
wrong: mktemp files are automatically backed up
Bash cannot write to an existing file
reasoning: Writing a new file and renaming it means readers see either the old or the new list. The answer adds undo and count using the same write_lines helper and four new checks.

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# todo.sh: a small task list kept in a plain text file.
set -euo pipefail

usage() {
    cat <<'TXT'
usage: todo.sh [-f FILE] COMMAND [ARGS]
commands:
  add TEXT...   append an open task
  list          show open tasks with their numbers
  complete N    mark task N as done
options:
  -f FILE       task file (default: $TODO_FILE, else ./todo.txt)
  -h, --help    show this help
TXT
}

die() {
    echo "todo: $1" >&2
    exit "${2:-1}"
}

# Replace the file in one rename so an interruption never leaves half a list.
write_lines() {
    local file=$1 tmp
    shift
    tmp=$(mktemp "$file.XXXXXX")
    # Copy first so the replacement keeps the original permissions (mktemp files are 0600).
    cp -p -- "$file" "$tmp"
    printf '%s\n' "$@" > "$tmp"
    mv -f -- "$tmp" "$file"
}

cmd_add() {
    (( $# )) || die 'add needs task text' 2
    printf '[ ] %s\n' "$*" >> "$file"
}

cmd_list() {
    [[ -f $file ]] || return 0
    local n=0 line
    while IFS= read -r line; do
        n=$((n + 1))
        if [[ $line == '[ ] '* ]]; then
            printf '%d. %s\n' "$n" "${line#'[ ] '}"
        fi
    done < "$file"
}

cmd_complete() {
    # Nine digits at most: longer numbers would overflow 64-bit arithmetic and wrap.
    [[ ${1-} =~ ^[1-9][0-9]{0,8}$ ]] || die 'complete needs a task number' 2
    [[ -f $file ]] || die "no tasks in $file"
    local lines i=$(($1 - 1))
    mapfile -t lines < "$file"
    (( i < ${#lines[@]} )) || die "no task $1"
    [[ ${lines[i]} == '[ ] '* ]] || die "task $1 is already done"
    lines[i]="[x] ${lines[i]#'[ ] '}"
    write_lines "$file" "${lines[@]}"
}

main() {
    file=${TODO_FILE:-todo.txt}
    if [[ ${1-} == --help ]]; then
        usage
        return
    fi
    local OPTIND opt
    while getopts ':f:h' opt; do
        case $opt in
            f) file=$OPTARG ;;
            h) usage; return ;;
            :) die "option -$OPTARG needs an argument" 2 ;;
            *) die "unknown option -$OPTARG" 2 ;;
        esac
    done
    shift $((OPTIND - 1))
    if (( $# == 0 )); then
        usage >&2
        exit 2
    fi
    local command=$1
    shift
    case $command in
        add) cmd_add "$@" ;;
        list) cmd_list ;;
        complete) cmd_complete "$@" ;;
        *) die "unknown command: $command" 2 ;;
    esac
}

main "$@"

title: Project: a streaming access-log analyzer
body: analyze.sh summarises web server logs in Common Log Format: total requests, malformed lines, bytes served, counts per status code and the busiest paths. It reads any number of files, or standard input when given no file or -, and streams line by line so input size is limited only by time.

Parsing uses one extended regular expression with capture groups and BASH_REMATCH instead of cut or awk per line, so no process is started per line. Malformed lines are counted and reported on stderr with their file name and line number; blank lines are ignored and a final line without a newline is still processed.

Counting uses associative arrays keyed by status and path. Log content is untrusted: keys are used only in assignments and ${...} expansions, never in eval, arithmetic subscripts or builtin arguments that re-expand them. A test feeds a path containing $(touch pwned) and checks that no file appears.

Reporting sorts keys explicitly because associative arrays have no order. Ranking pipes counts into sort and reads the full result with mapfile, then slices the first TOP entries in Bash. Using head here would let sort die from SIGPIPE, which pipefail and errexit would turn into a failed run.

Exercise levels — Beginner: run the suite and explain each line of the expected report. Intermediate: add a -e option for monitoring that exits with status 3 when any 5xx response was seen, explaining the reason on stderr. Advanced: decide where the Bash loop stops being fast enough and compare with an awk version on a million generated lines. The worked answer implements -e with three new checks.
A mutation check reverses the ranking order; the suite must fail, showing that the report test pins the ordering, not just the counts.

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# analyze.sh: summarise web server access logs in Common Log Format.
set -euo pipefail

usage() {
    echo 'usage: analyze.sh [-n TOP] [FILE...]   (reads stdin when no FILE is given or FILE is -)'
}

die() {
    echo "analyze: $1" >&2
    exit "${2:-1}"
}

# 203.0.113.9 - - [16/Oct/2026:10:00:00 +0000] "GET /index.html HTTP/1.1" 200 512
line_re='^[^ ]+ [^ ]+ [^ ]+ \[[^]]+\] "([A-Z]+) ([^ "]+)[^"]*" ([0-9]{3}) ([0-9]+|-)$'

declare -A by_status=() by_path=()
requests=0 malformed=0 bytes=0

# Log text is data: keys are only used in assignments and ${...}, never re-parsed.
analyze_stream() {
    local name=$1 line n=0 status path size
    while IFS= read -r line || [[ -n $line ]]; do
        n=$((n + 1))
        if [[ $line =~ $line_re ]]; then
            path=${BASH_REMATCH[2]} status=${BASH_REMATCH[3]} size=${BASH_REMATCH[4]}
            requests=$((requests + 1))
            by_status[$status]=$(( ${by_status[$status]:-0} + 1 ))
            by_path[$path]=$(( ${by_path[$path]:-0} + 1 ))
            [[ $size == - ]] || bytes=$((bytes + size))
        elif [[ -n $line ]]; then
            malformed=$((malformed + 1))
            echo "analyze: $name:$n: malformed line" >&2
        fi
    done
}

report() {
    local top=$1 code path ranked=() entry
    echo "requests: $requests"
    echo "malformed: $malformed"
    echo "bytes: $bytes"
    echo 'status:'
    if (( ${#by_status[@]} )); then
        while IFS= read -r code; do
            printf '  %s %d\n' "$code" "${by_status[$code]}"
        done < <(printf '%s\n' "${!by_status[@]}" | sort)
    fi
    echo "top $top paths:"
    if (( ${#by_path[@]} )); then
        # Sort everything, then slice in Bash: head would SIGPIPE sort under pipefail.
        mapfile -t ranked < <(for path in "${!by_path[@]}"; do
            printf '%d\t%s\n' "${by_path[$path]}" "$path"
        done | sort -t $'\t' -k1,1nr -k2,2)
        for entry in "${ranked[@]:0:top}"; do
            printf '  %d %s\n' "${entry%%$'\t'*}" "${entry#*$'\t'}"
        done
    fi
}

main() {
    local top=3 opt OPTIND file
    while getopts ':n:h' opt; do
        case $opt in
            # Six digits at most keeps the later array slice far from integer overflow.
            n) [[ $OPTARG =~ ^[1-9][0-9]{0,5}$ ]] || die '-n needs a number from 1 to 999999' 2
               top=$OPTARG ;;
            h) usage; return ;;
            *) usage >&2; exit 2 ;;
        esac
    done
    shift $((OPTIND - 1))
    (( $# )) || set -- -
    for file in "$@"; do
        if [[ $file == - ]]; then
            analyze_stream stdin
        elif [[ -f $file && -r $file ]]; then
            # shellcheck disable=SC2094  # the name is only a label for messages
            analyze_stream "$file" < "$file"
        else
            die "cannot read $file"
        fi
    done
    report "$top"
}

main "$@"

title: Project: an atomic, locked configuration updater
body: setconf.sh sets KEY=VALUE in a configuration file. It keeps comments, blank lines and ordering, appends new keys, reports added, updated or unchanged, supports a dry run and creates the file when it does not exist.

Safety is the theme. The key is validated against an allow-list pattern and values containing newlines are rejected, so input cannot add extra lines. The new content is rendered into a mktemp file in the same directory and moved over the original in one atomic rename.

The temporary file is created by copying the original with cp -p first, so the replacement keeps the original permissions — a config readable only by its group stays that way. A plain mktemp file would silently become mode 600; when the file is new, the script applies the normal umask-derived mode instead. Duplicate keys are all rewritten, and any differing copy counts as an update, so the tool never reports unchanged while a stale value remains.

Concurrency: a lock directory created with mkdir guarantees only one writer at a time; a second writer fails immediately with status 75 (EX_TEMPFAIL, "try again later"). An EXIT trap removes the temporary file and the lock in every outcome, and a test checks nothing is left behind.

Exercise levels — Beginner: run the tests and explain why the special-character value is stored literally. Intermediate: add -d KEY to delete a key, reporting deleted or absent. #!/usr/bin/env bash
# setconf.sh: set KEY=VALUE in a config file atomically, under a lock.
set -euo pipefail

usage() {
    echo 'usage: setconf.sh [-n] [-f FILE] KEY VALUE   (-n: dry run; default FILE: app.conf)'
}

die() {
    echo "setconf: $1" >&2
    exit "${2:-1}"
}

tmp='' lock=''
cleanup() {
    [[ -n $tmp ]] && rm -f -- "$tmp"
    [[ -n $lock ]] && rmdir -- "$lock"
    return 0
}
trap cleanup EXIT

acquire_lock() {
    # mkdir is atomic: exactly one process can create the directory.
    if mkdir -- "$1.lock" 2>/dev/null; then
        lock=$1.lock
    else
        die "$1 is locked by another process" 75
    fi
}

# Print the new file contents and set result to added, updated or unchanged.
render() {
    local key=$1 value=$2 file=$3 line found=0 differs=0
    result=added
    if [[ -f $file ]]; then
        while IFS= read -r line || [[ -n $line ]]; do
            if [[ $line == "$key="* ]]; then
                found=1
                # Every duplicate is rewritten, so any differing copy means the file changes.
                [[ ${line#*=} == "$value" ]] || differs=1
                printf '%s=%s\n' "$key" "$value"
            else
                printf '%s\n' "$line"
            fi
        done < "$file"
    fi
    if (( found )); then
        if (( differs )); then result=updated; else result=unchanged; fi
    else
        printf '%s=%s\n' "$key" "$value"
    fi
}

main() {
    local file=app.conf dry_run=0 opt OPTIND
    while getopts ':nf:h' opt; do
        case $opt in
            n) dry_run=1 ;;
            f) file=$OPTARG ;;
            h) usage; return ;;
            *) usage >&2; exit 2 ;;
        esac
    done
    shift $((OPTIND - 1))
    (( $# == 2 )) || { usage >&2; exit 2; }
    local key=$1 value=$2
    [[ $key =~ ^[A-Za-z_][A-Za-z0-9_.]*$ ]] || die "invalid key: $key" 2
    [[ $value != *$'\n'* ]] || die 'values cannot contain newlines' 2

    acquire_lock "$file"
    local dir=.
    [[ $file == */* ]] && dir=${file%/*}
    tmp=$(mktemp "$dir/.setconf.XXXXXX")
    # Copy first so the replacement keeps the original permissions.
    if [[ -f $file ]]; then
        cp -p -- "$file" "$tmp"
    else
        # A new file gets the usual umask-based mode, not mktemp's private 0600.
        chmod "$(printf '%o' $(( 0666 & ~$(umask) )))" "$tmp"
    fi
    render "$key" "$value" "$file" > "$tmp"
    if (( dry_run )); then
        echo "would be $result: $key"
    elif [[ $result == unchanged ]]; then
        echo "unchanged: $key"
    else
        mv -f -- "$tmp" "$file"
        tmp=''
        echo "$result: $key"
    fi

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# prun.sh: run COMMAND once per input with at most JOBS running at a time.
set -euo pipefail

usage() {
    echo 'usage: prun.sh [-j JOBS] [-0] -- COMMAND [ARGS...]   (inputs on stdin, one per line or NUL-separated with -0)'
}

die() {
    echo "prun: $1" >&2
    exit "${2:-1}"
}

out=$(mktemp -d)
trap 'rm -rf -- "$out"' EXIT

# Wait for any one job, record its status by input index and free a slot.
collect() {
    local finished status=0
    wait -n -p finished || status=$?
    statuses[${index_of[$finished]}]=$status
    unset "index_of[$finished]"
    running=$((running - 1))
}

main() {
    local jobs=2 delimiter=$'\n' opt OPTIND
    while getopts ':j:0h' opt; do
        case $opt in
            j) [[ $OPTARG =~ ^[1-9][0-9]*$ ]] || die '-j needs a positive number' 2
               jobs=$OPTARG ;;
            0) delimiter='' ;;
            h) usage; return ;;
            *) usage >&2; exit 2 ;;
        esac
    done
    shift $((OPTIND - 1))
    (( $# )) || { usage >&2; exit 2; }

    local inputs=() statuses=() i running=0 ok=0 failed=0
    local -A index_of=()
    mapfile -t -d "$delimiter" inputs
    for i in "${!inputs[@]}"; do
        (( running < jobs )) || collect
        # Each job writes to its own file, so concurrent output never interleaves.
        "$@" "${inputs[i]}" > "$out/$i" 2>&1 &
        index_of[$!]=$i
        running=$((running + 1))
    done
    while (( running )); do collect; done

    for i in "${!inputs[@]}"; do
        cat -- "$out/$i"
        if (( statuses[i] == 0 )); then
            ok=$((ok + 1))
        else
            failed=$((failed + 1))
            printf 'prun: %q failed with status %d\n' "${inputs[i]}" "${statuses[i]}" >&2
        fi
    done
    echo "prun: $ok ok, $failed failed" >&2
    (( failed == 0 ))
}

main "$@"

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# prun.sh: run COMMAND once per input with at most JOBS running at a time.
set -euo pipefail

usage() {
    echo 'usage: prun.sh [-j JOBS] [-0] [-f] -- COMMAND [ARGS...]   (inputs on stdin, one per line or NUL-separated with -0; -f stops starting jobs after a failure)'
}

die() {
    echo "prun: $1" >&2
    exit "${2:-1}"
}

out=$(mktemp -d)
trap 'rm -rf -- "$out"' EXIT

record() {
    statuses[${index_of[$1]}]=$2
    unset "index_of[$1]"
    running=$((running - 1))
    (( $2 == 0 )) || any_failed=1
}

# Wait for any one job, record its status by input index and free a slot.
collect() {
    local finished status=0 pid
    wait -n -p finished || status=$?
    record "$finished" "$status"
    # Fail fast must also see failures among other jobs that have already ended.
    if (( fail_fast )); then
        for pid in "${!index_of[@]}"; do
            kill -0 "$pid" 2>/dev/null && continue
            status=0
            wait "$pid" || status=$?
            record "$pid" "$status"
        done
    fi
}

main() {
    local jobs=2 delimiter=$'\n' fail_fast=0 opt OPTIND
    while getopts ':j:0fh' opt; do
        case $opt in
            j) [[ $OPTARG =~ ^[1-9][0-9]*$ ]] || die '-j needs a positive number' 2
               jobs=$OPTARG ;;
            0) delimiter='' ;;
            f) fail_fast=1 ;;
            h) usage; return ;;
            *) usage >&2; exit 2 ;;
        esac
    done
    shift $((OPTIND - 1))
    (( $# )) || { usage >&2; exit 2; }

    local inputs=() statuses=() i running=0 ok=0 failed=0 skipped=0 any_failed=0
    local -A index_of=()
    mapfile -t -d "$delimiter" inputs
    for i in "${!inputs[@]}"; do
        (( running < jobs )) || collect
        (( fail_fast && any_failed )) && break
        # Each job writes to its own file, so concurrent output never interleaves.
        "$@" "${inputs[i]}" > "$out/$i" 2>&1 &
        index_of[$!]=$i
        running=$((running + 1))
    done
    while (( running )); do collect; done

    for i in "${!inputs[@]}"; do
        if [[ ! -v statuses[i] ]]; then
            skipped=$((skipped + 1))
            continue
        fi
        cat -- "$out/$i"
        if (( statuses[i] == 0 )); then
            ok=$((ok + 1))
        else
            failed=$((failed + 1))
            printf 'prun: %q failed with status %d\n' "${inputs[i]}" "${statuses[i]}" >&2
        fi
    done
    if (( skipped )); then
        echo "prun: $ok ok, $failed failed, $skipped skipped" >&2
    else
        echo "prun: $ok ok, $failed failed" >&2
    fi
    (( failed == 0 ))
}

main "$@"

title: Capstone: a verified, rotating backup tool
body: The capstone brings everything together in backup.sh SOURCE DEST: it creates a timestamped tar.gz of a directory, verifies it can be read, keeps the newest KEEP archives, supports a dry run and refuses to run twice at once. Treat it as a reference for structuring production shell tools.

Robustness: set -eEuo pipefail with an ERR trap reports the failing command and line; an EXIT trap removes the temporary archive and lock in every outcome; destructive operations use -- and quoted, checked paths; exit statuses distinguish usage (2), failure (1) and a held lock (75). Diagnostics go to stderr while stdout carries only the archive path, so callers can capture it.

Atomicity: tar writes into a mktemp file in the destination directory, tar -tzf reads it back, and only then mv publishes it under its final name. A crash or failure never leaves a truncated archive with a real-looking name, and an existing archive is never overwritten.

Testability: BACKUP_NOW overrides the clock, so tests produce exact names. Rotation relies on timestamps that sort lexicographically — a deliberate naming choice that makes glob order chronological on any Bash (GLOBSORT=name would make it explicit on 5.3). The rotation glob spells out the stamp shape, so backing up data never deletes archives of a different source named data-old; a dry run counts the archive it would create, so it lists exactly what a real run deletes. Tests restore an archive and compare it with diff -r, exercise rotation, dry run, locking, invalid input and a real tar failure caught by the ERR trap.
